SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

INGENIOUS ARRANGEMENT FOR TRAM CARS.—On the Hamburg tearaways a number of cars with ftangeless wheels, much like omnibuses, and with turning gear, are working. To run on the lines, these cars are fitted with a shaft in front of the front wheels, this shaft carrying on a lever a disc wheel which the driver can lower into the tramrail groove as he requires, or raise it when it is necessary to get out of the way of obstructions. The arrangement works well, saves a lot of trouble, and the cars run easier than those with flanged wheels. A FRENCH CENTENARIAN.—Mr. Vereker, British Consul at Cherbourg, writes :—"The following instance of longevity is fully authenticated :—Monsieur Gilles Louis Bouillle, born May 10, 1781, died at Caen on the 21st of June, being thus in his 103rd year; he had been President of the Tribunal of Commerce of Caen, Administrator of Hospitals and Town Councillor at same place, was a Knight of the Legion of Honour, and had the St. Helena medal. I am informed by the late Monsieur Bouillie's family that he enjoyed good health and unimpaired faculties to the last." SURVIVAL OF THE FITTEST P—An American papericites a case in which Darwin's doctrine of the survival of the fittest was not substantiated. On a New Jersey farm there were fifty chickens, one of the number being lame. In a struggle for the food supply the lame chicken would be at a disad- vantage, and therefore ought, in accordance with the doc- trine, to die out, lameness being thus eliminated from the species. But some malicious member of another species one day poisoned the food given to the chickens. The forty-nine vigorous birds greedily swallowed allethe supply—and died; while the lame chicken, which was distanced in the struggle, lived on. PILE DlVELLlNGS.—Excavations which have recently been made in moorland, near Billigheim, in the Palatinate, have afforded evidence of the former existence there of pile dwellings, dating from the stone age, and apparently used also in the Middle Ages. Stone implements made of flint and jasper have been found, but along with them tabular bricks apparently belonging to the thirteenth century. Pile dwellings, which served as strongholds as late as the Middle Ages, are well known to have been found in the formerly Slavonic part of north-east Germany. IN ODD FELLOW. (roll TO WILL AT SARATOGA.) Yes, as you say, they're charming girls, Bright, ladydike, and witty, And whether they wear bangs or curls, They're all uncoaitnon pretty. And then they dress so well, 'tis clear They think it's woman's duty To study just what kind of gear Will most enhance her beauty. But really I begin to find The place a trifle dreary— Of so much lovlineas combined, Old chap, I'm growing weary. And trath to tell, I'd like to see A girl a wee bit homely; Fan sure it would refreshing be, Among a host so comely. And I oat thinking of one now: lier 1:1062—well, it is funny, And though the sun has kissed her brow, Her tresses are not sunny; Nor are her eyes of wondrous size, Like some that I've seen lately; And while she with no fairy vies, She's neither tall nor stately. Her laughter wakes the echoes, and She's altogether jolly; No diamonds sparkle on her hand; Her name's not "May," but " Molly She never sounds the final" g," Says " puddin'," " walkin'," " stunnin'," And speaks no French, and yet to me, By Jove! she's awful cunnin'. And though these girls much loyelier are— In fact, with graces laden— I'd rather have, I would by far, My little homely maiden. —Hoeper's Weekly. MARGARET ETYNGE.

THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY JULY 28 1883.
NOTES ON —AGRICULTURE, HORTI- CULTURE, &c.

Some plants of rye, varying in length from 6ft. to 7ft., and having remarkably fine ears have been plucked by Mr. C. Humphrey, Fordham, Downlam Market. The fruit crop in some parts of Kent is unprecedented. Strawberries have been sold at 6d. per gallon in order to keep growth under, as the markets have been over supplied. SHEAF-BINDER TRIALS.—At the trial of sheaf-binders, from June 25 to 30, 1883, at Grosseto, Italy, the Mc.Cor- mick machine was awarded the first prize, a gold medal and 1,000 lire and also the Diploma of Honour, by the Minister of Agriculture. THE LARGEST TENANT-FARMER IN ENGLAND.—At Kenil- worth Divisional Sessions, Mr. Chas. Frederick Trepplin, who occupies twelve farms, and was described as the largest tenant-farmer in England, was charged with having neg- lected to report to the police that he had foot and mouth disease on his Villiers-hill Farm. The defence was that the disease was reported as soon as recognised. The Bench fined the defendant £lO, and Zl us. 6d. of expenses. "SAMPLING" A COUNTRY.—According to the Pzttsburg Stockman Western Michigan will attack cattle shows in the East this fall with an advertising car. The plan is to put speci- mens of grain,fruit,pumpkins,ores and other products in the car to show the vegetable and mineral richness of the region, take a professor or two from the agricultural college to give the thing tone, and visit as many fairs as possible in New England and the Middle States. A very enterprising way of sampling a country, truly. VEGETARIAN CHEESE RENNET.—Earnest vegetarians who do not repudiate cheese have been seriously troubled by the necessity of using the stomachs of slaughtered calves as a source of the rennet which is used in making the curd, and many attempts to supersede the animal coagulant by using vegetable and mineral acids, alum, &c., have failed. They will doubtless be glad to learn, on the authority of Sir Wm. Hooker, that a shrub common in Northern India supplies a vegetable rennet. Its name is Puneeria cogulan's. A decoc- tion of 30 parts of its powdered capsules in 1,150 parts of water is a coagulating liquid of such strength that a tea- spoonful is sufficient for curdlinga gallon of milk, or, other- wise stated, the quantity required is one teaspoonful of the powder to 38 gallons of milk. AGRICULTURE IN CANADA.— According to the third volume of the Canadian Census of 1881, the number of per- sons returned as occupiers of the land in 1881 was 464,025, having increased from 367,862 in 1871; 403,491 were re- turned as owners' and 57,245 as tenants, 3,789 being em- ployes. The total number of acres occupied was 45,358,141, compared with 36,046,401 in 1871, of which 29,899,181 were improved land, 15,112,284 were under crops, and 6,385,562 in pasture. There were 643,171 horses, 201,253 colts and fillies, 132,593 working 0xen,1,159,800 mulch cows, 1,786,596 other horned cattle, 3,048,678 sheep, 1,206,617 swine. .The produce of cereals and other crops were as fol- lows :—Wheat, 32,350,260 bushels; barley, 16,844,868 bushels; oats, 70,493,131; rye, 2,097,180; peas and beans, 13,749,662; Indian c0rn,9,025,142 ; potatoes, 55,268,227: turnips, 39,659,094; besides 9,192,320 bushels of other roots. A REMEDY FOR FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE.—Mr. W. Hogg, grazier, Tranent, writes to a contemporary :—On the 4th of April last I bathed five sheep out of a flock of over 300, amongst which the disease had commenced, and they all took it except these five. Eleven weeks have now passed since then, and they are still unaffected, whiok gives me good reason to believe that the mixture I used has been an effectual preventive of that disease. I first rubbed Arch- angel tar into the glands of the feet and round the muzzle and nostrils; and for each sheep I made a mixture, consist- ing of a wine-glassful of spirits of tar, the same of tobacco liquor, and 70 grains of hellebore, this being first mixed up in a cupful of boiling water). A quart of cold water is then added, and the preparation is ready for use. I poured it on, as it is the safest way, each sheep getting its own proper share of the ingredients. Cattle can be treated in 1 the same way, and with the same desired effect, if done while they are still uncontaminated. SALE OF SHORTHORNS.—An important sale of shorthorn cattle was held at Castle-hill, Cerne Abbas, on Wednesday afternoon week, by Mr. John Thornton the stock offered being the property of Mr. T. Holford, high sheriff of Dor- setshire. Mr. Holford has long been noted for the high character of his herd, and the great prices obtained show that his reputation was deserved. Earl Bective gave 500 guineas for Airdrie Duchess 7th and 1,505 guineas for Duchess of Leicester, Lord Fitzhardinge securing Duchess of Leicester 3rd for 1,150 guineas. Two Oxfords brought 320 and 420 guineas respectively, and another Leicester 355 guineas. The Duke of Leicester went to Lord Fitzbardinge , for 900 guineas, and the Duke of Leicester 4th, just a year old, realised 205 guineas; while Duke of Leicester 6th, a ' very fine large calf, born in March last, brought the extra- ordinary price of 355 guineas; 32 cows brought 5,632 guineas, being an average of 176 guineas. Five bulls, 1,611 guineas, or 322 guineas average. The total of the sale was 7,362 guineas. , FEEDING HORSES -BY MACHINERY.—Mr. Henry Pitman writes :—" For reasons of humanity and utility, I ask leave to mention to your readers a novel contrivance for feeding I horses and cattle by machinery. I understand that horses can be groomed by machinery, but I have not seen the pro- cess; I can, however, testify that it is practicable and bene- ficial to feed these useful animals 'automatically.' When I first heard of this invention, I said to myself, Surely , such a simple work as giving horses their food does not need mechanical contrivance.' I found, on inspecting the apparatus, that it deserves adoption on the grounds of health, economy, and humanity. When I was a boy, my father now and then gave me a drive, and I remember that he always went into the stable to see his horse fed. Seeing is believing.' He objected to pay for a feed' when the horse didn't get it. This contrivance will help to prevent the dishonest trick of robbing horses of their oats; because now any number of them can be fed at a fixed time, even when the stable door is locked. From a humanitarian point of view, this ingenious contrivance has other recommenda- tions. Regularity in meals, with ample time for mastica- tion and digestion, is as essential to the health of horses as of human beings. Now it is a deplorable fact that thou- sands of horses are daily taken out to work either without having been fed, or with only a few minutes for their morning meal. Such neglect is cruel, and injurious to the horses. These considerations led Mr. J. P. Milbourne, of Manchester, to construct clockwork apparatus by which horses can be fed at a fixed time in the absence of the stableman. The inventor says :—'Armed with this appara- tus, owners of horses have an efficient guarantee that their horses will be fed sufficiently early before being yoked.' The invention can be applied to the 'feeding of cattle as well as horses. The apparatus, which is simple and inexpensive, is set in motion by a clock, and at the appointed moment the food falls down a shoot into the manger, either at once or in two portions, with an interval of half an hour. Water can be supplied as well as food. The invention is appicable to other purposes, such as opening or closing dampers in steam boilers, turning off gas, opening sluices, &c. The in- ventor will show his patent at work, and send an illustrated description freely to any applicant. Address, Mr. J. P. Milburne, 5, Eastnor-street, Cornbrook, Manchester."

A traveller in a stage coach not famed for its celerity in- quired the name of the coach. "I think, sir," said a fellow passenger, "it must be the Regulator, for I observe all the other coaches go by it." "What are you going to do when you grow up if you don't know how to cipher ?" asked a Board school teacher of a rather slow boy. "I'm going to be a teacher, and make the boys do the ciphering," was the reply. A SISTER OF THOMAS CARLYLE.—The Detroit (Michi- gan) Post gives an interesting account of a sister of Thomas Carlyle :—Mrs. Janet Carlyle Hanning, Hamilton, Ontario, was a rnest at the Griswold House yesterday, and the favoured few who were in the secret were not long in pay- ing their respects to the sister of the famous philosopher, the late Thomas Carlyle. Mrs. Hanning is a small, slight lady, with a gentle and benign expression of countenance and the keen, bright eyes which betoken that clear-sighted- ness peculiar to the Scotch people. Honesty and a severe integrity also characterise her expression, and she has a gentle brogue, or accent, which is very fascinating. The idiom of the lowland Scotch, which crops out in an occa- sional word, is happy and pithy, in concealing rather than expressing thought. Being very tired with her journey, and this being her first visit to "the States," Mrs. Hanning excused herself and retired early, leaving to her son-in-law, Mr. George M. Franklin, the duty of answering inquiries. "My mother-in-law," said Mr. Franklin, "is the second youngest sister of Thomas Carlyle, and was the favourite one at home. Being the finest needlewoman in the family, all the nicest sewing was done by her after her return home from boarding-school. This was at Scotsburg, where they lived at that time, haying moved from Ecclefechan before Janet was born. Mrs. Hanning had lived in Canada 35 years; her husband was a draper in Manchester, but he could not make a success of that business and emigrated to Canada. He has been dead now for five years. My wife is next to the youngest of her family. Mrs. Hanning brought up her four daughters to work. Thera is no kind of house- work that they cannot do. She herself has done all her own work, even to her washing, until within the last few years. Why, when Ralph Waldo Emerson called on her she was cooking dinner, but she wouldn't ask him to stay. I couldn't,' she said, 'ask Mr. Emerson to sit down to a stew." "Does Mrs. Hanning keep up her interest in her distin- guished brother?" "She does indeed, and she has brought up her family to revere the name of Carlyle; she has a letter written by him to his mother on the death of his father. It is the most beautiful and pathetic thing ever written. Some , day the letters she has from Uncle Tom will make a finer collection than anything of his that has yet been published. Not one of them has ever been mutilated. When Mr. Han- ning died, a Detroit gentleman with whom she was ac- quainted wrote and solicited an autograph of Carlyle's. She gave it, but only owing to the peculiar circumstances." "Did Mr. Carlyle remember her in his will ?" " Yes ; she was one of five residuary legatees. Dr. John Carlyle, who had previously died, had also remembered her. She has many rare and valuable—l can say priceless—relics of her brother Thomas, personal property, and a set of volumes of his history of Frederick the Great, with her name written by him on every blank page." Temperance seems on the increase, if we may judge by the extraordinary demand for the Montserrat Lime Juice; over 100,000 galloAs being imported annually. The Lancet says :—'• The Mentserrat is purest, and we counsel the public to drink it. As a rule, Lime Juice is, particularly during the summer, a far more wholesome drink than any form of alcohol. We have subjected the samples of the 'Lime Fruit Juice' of the Montserrat Company to full analysis, to test its quality and purity. We hare found it to be in sound condition, and entirely free from adulteration." MONTSERRAT Lime Fruit Juice and Cordials. Limetta or Pure lime Juice Cordials, Aromatic' Clove, Etrawberry, Raspberry, Sarsaparilla, Pine- apple, Jargonelle, Peppermint, Quinine, &C.—Advt.

• . COTTAGE GARDENING. CABBAGE.—A small sowing of such varieties as Non- pareil, Early York, and Cattell's Reliance should be made now. Select for the purpose a moderately-rich and friable piece of ground. Open drills one inch deep and 6in. dis- 1 tant ; sow the seeds thinly in these, and cover the seed over by simply filling or levelling the drills, breaking the soil as fine as possible as the work proceeds. We would remind our readers that unless they are secured by a net the chances are a hundred to one that they will not see a single plant come up. A week or a fortnight lost at this time of the year is highly important; make sure, therefore, of the first sowing. Osioss.—We have already prepared the ground for the sowing of Winter Onions. We have selected a piece of ground lying open to the sun. It was trenched last year 3ft. deep, and well manured. We have added some more this season, as it was dug—the surface having been im- poverished by a small crop or two—otherwise, we are not partial to supplying onions with too much fresh manure near the surface. PARSLEY.—We have made a small sowing of this during this week. Some we scattered amongst turnips ready for pulling, and by the time the turnips are cleared we hope to see the parsley nearly covering the ground. Another bed was sown in a south aspect. The seeds were simply scat- tered on the surface, and afterwards trod in. No time should now be lost in making up any blanks in the various crops of winter vegetables such as kails, savoys, &c. All kinds of vegetables intended for exhibition should be kept well thinned out, so that they do not overcrowd each other. Plenty of space has much to do with fine specimens of all kind of vegetables. Tanking vegetables, or supplyingrihem with manure water, is not so well understood as it should be. Asa rule, its application should be confined to that period in a plant's existence when there is the greatest strain on its energies. This, as a rule, occurs when a plant is flowering or forming its seed. It is notorious that plants in a sickly state are seldom benefited by an application of manure water. The reason is obvious. Plants in such a condition have few or weakly roots and as the roots are the agents that absorb the liquids add conduct it to the system of the plant, their feebleness of action naturally allows the liquid to remain in the soil, doing more harm than good, inasmuch that its presence sours the soil. Anyone can select a plant in a pot and ascertain this for themselves. We may reason- ably conclude that manure water is of use in proportion to the quantity of roots there are to utilise it, and is more beneficial to maintain a healthy, vigorous constitution, which might otherwise succumb, than it is to excite to action a debilitated vegetation. An important rule in supplying plants with liquid manure should be observed, i.e., to apply it weak and often. We have seen plants permanently in- jured through having too strong doses of manure water. FRONT GARDEN.— The earliest-sown Sweet William, Wallflowers, Canterbury Bells, and Columbines should now be ready for picking out. We have put ours in the vegetable garden in beds, allowing 6in, space between each plant. From here they will be moved in the spring, and planted where they are to flower. PlNKS.—Cuttings or pipings of these should now be secured and placed in a shady corner, and if covered with glass, as we previously hinted, few will fail to root. The pipings are made about 3in. long, severing them at a joint that is moderately firm, or, if not too long, use them as they are stripped off the plant. We like to trim with a sharp knife the first pair of lowest leaves clean off, considering that they have a tendency to hasten decay in the cutting. If glass is placed over the pipings, it is not necessary that it should be kept close at all times. It may be partially moved at night after the first week, and occasionally on dull days. The object is to maintain the cuttings from flag- ging. Propagating boxes, such as we have suggested more than once, fulfil this requirement by checking evaporation ' from the surface of the leaves. Should the sun get on the • glass for any length of time, a sheet of paper secured on the • glass will intercept its rays. GERANDDIS.—Cuttings of the bedding out varieties made now, and inserted in the open ground, even by the aide of the parent plant, will root readily and make good plants by the end of August. One or two cuttings now will be of more value to the cottager than half-a-dozen in a month's ' time. They should be taken off judiciously—for instance, a shoot that extends itself much beyond the ethers should , be selected first, and severed just where the wood is mode- rately hard. Cut the bottom of it even just below the , joint, and remove the lower leaves with a knife. THE Wisrnow.—Passing through the eastern outskirts of ' Leyland, we noticed the other day four cottage windows ' very gay. Boxes had been made to fit on the window ledge, apparently no more than Gin. wide. The sides facing the : road were covered over with virgin cork, thus clothing bare smooth boards with artistic ruggedness. The plants in the boxes were scarlet geraniums, yellow calceolarias, blue lobelia, and a variegated grass (dactylis glomerata), and their appearance reflected great credit on the owners. Scarlet and pink geraniums and blue lobelias make a nice box, with a plant of canary creeper or nasturtium at'nach end to train up the window sides. A piece of string secured at the top, middle, and bottom will afford support for them. It is a mistake to have the string too loose, for in that case the wind has more power on the plant, which keeps it con- tinually moving, which may ultimately result in it being twisted right off at the bottom. HYDRANGEAS, of which we are pleased to see a few grown, should as soon as they appear shabby be cut well down. Upon examining the shoot—that is, the flowering shoot—there will be found at the base some prominent buds. Cut down to these, though they may he but two or three inches from the pot. Should there be a shoot or two that have not flowered allow them to remain, and place the plant in the sunniest position outside. The wood will get ma- tured, and they will most probably set plump buds at the points, which will produce two corymbs the following season almost large enough to fill an ordinary sized window.
Dealers in antiquities will pay a big price for the last straw which broke the camel's back.

COURAGE.—Papa: "Glad to see you to-morrow evening. My daughter Alice will sing, and Beatrice will recite to us a new Poem she's composed. We sup at Niue."—Young Man : "Thanks! You're very kind. 'Most happy. I'll be with you at Nine."'—Punch. THE CUNNING OF THE Fox.—Abundance of evidence exists testifying to the unrivalled cunning of the fox. Both in avoiding danger and procuring food he exhibits a craft that is really remarkable. His senses, of course, are ex- tremely keen. It has been stated that the shepherds of Thrace ascertain whether a frozen river will "bear" or not by sending a fox across. The creature is observed to place the side of its head upon the ice, as if listening for the flow of water underneath, and should it cross, it is considered safe to follow its example. The difficulty of catching foxes by means of traps is notorious. They seem to have an in- stinctive knack of spying a snare; and iron in any shape or form is avoided with such pertinacity as to render the ma- terial almost useless in the construction of a trap. More- over, they are just as acute in approaching their prey as they are in escaping themselves. They have been seen to swim slowly towards water-fowl with a turf in their mouth, so as not only to remain hidden, but to avoid attracting attention. Foxes caught red-handed—that is, in the very act of theft or murder—have been known to imitate death, and to submit to a great amount of rough handling in the chance of an opportunity of escape presenting itself. In- stances are on record where a fox, tracked to its hole— which had been surrounded by traps—has endured starva- tion for many days rather than come out of hiding, and so be captured. Truly, an animal which could readily take in the situation at a glance must be acknowledged to be the king of cunning creatures.—Front Little Folks. ERNST.—At this time Jenny Lind and Ernst were both in London, and Liszt, I believe, passed through like a meteor. I never heard any of them in their prime, though I did hear Madame Lind-Goldschmidt sing "The Ravens" at a concert years afterwards, and it was my privilege to hear Ernst before he had lost his cunning, nor shall I ever hear his like again. He played once at Her Majesty's Opera House, when the whole assembly seemed to dream through a performance of the "Hungarian Airs." The lightest whisper of the violin controlled the house; the magician hardly stirred his wand at times, and no one could tell from the sound when he passed from the up to the down bow in those long cantabile notes which had such power to en- trance me. I heard him later at Brighton. He played out of tune, and I was told that he was so shaken in nerve that playing a Beethoven quartet in private, and coming to a passage of the first violin of no great difficulty, which I have often scrambled through with impunity, the great master laid down his fiddle and declared himself unequal to the effort. Great, deep-sonled, weird magician of the Cre- mona! I can see the pale, gaunt face even now! Those dark, haggard-looking eyes, with the strange veiled fires, semi-mesmeric, the wasted hands, so expressive and sensi- tive, the thin lank hair and emaciated form, yet withal nothing demoniac about thee like Paganini, from whom thou want absolutely distinct! No copy thou, thyself all thyself—tender, sympathetic, gentle as a child, suffering, always sufferinf ; full of an excessive sensibility; full of charm; irresistible and fascinating beyond words! Thy Cremona should hare been buried with thee! It has fallen into other hands. I see it every season in the concert-room: Madame Norman-Neruda plays it. I know she is an admir- able artiste. Ido not hear thy Cremona; its voice has gone out with thee, its soul has passed with thine! In the night I hear it under the stars, when the moon is low, and I see the dark ridges of the clover hills, and rabbits and hares, black against the paler sky, pausing to feed or crouching to listen to the voices of the night. Alone in the autumn woods, when through the shivering trees I see the angry yellow streaks of the sunset, and the dead leaves fall across a sky that threatens storm. By the sea, when the cold mists rise, and hollow murmurs, like the low wail of lost spirits, rush along the beach. In some still valley in the South, in midsummer, the slate-coloured moth on the rock flashes suddenly into crimson and takes wing; the bright-eyed lizard darts timorously, and the singing of the grasshopper never ceases in the long grass; the air is heavy and slum- berous with insect life and the breath of flowers. I can see the blue sky—intense blue—mirrored in the lake, and a bird floats mirrored in the blue, and over the shining water comes the sound, breaking the singing silences of nature; such things are in our dreams! It is thus only I can hear again the spirit voice of thy Cremona, dead master, but not at St. James' Hall; no longer in the crowded haunts of men as once, its body only is there; its soul was the very soul of the master who has passed to where the chiming is "after the chiming of the eternal spheres."—Rev. H. R. Haweis, in "The Gentleman's Magazine." THE PRINTER'S DEVIL.-VIII. [thr ANGLO•SCOTUSJ (The right of re-publication is reserved) Under the term "Primrose," books of reference on out-of- the-way subjects record the fact that "this common little plant [primula vulgaris] affords an extraordinary example of blundering." The erratic peculiarities or influences of the plants Wordsworth has sung about would seem to be contagious. The relative size of a bunch of them taken into a house, in some parts of the country, is believed or supposed to influence for good or evil the broods of young ducks; and properly manipulated, it is believed in other parts that the stamens of the flower will enable a youth or maiden to secure a sweetheart to their individual liking. Again, some of those individuals who have borne the name of "Primrose" have been credited with possessing peculiar powers and curious notions. One Dr. Primrose was vain of his theory on second marriages, and was given to smashing bottled " washes " with a kitchen poker; his wife was very proud of her recipe for making gooseberry wine; and their son, totally ignorant of the Dutch language, went to Amsterdam to teach English. Then there was the cele- brated Moses of that ilk who bartered the horse for a gross ' of green spectacles; and the "soft, modest, and alluring" Sophia, who secured for herself a husband by means of a spirited horse and a tumble into deep water. But all these peculiarities or Powers fade into ineignificance before the attributes accorded to Archibald Philip Primrose, fifth Earl of Rosebery, by a Birmingham compositor and reader. The two last-named worthies, to paraphrase the words of Shake- speare, must have contemptuously ignored "the steep and thorny way to correctness," and Like puffed and reckless libertines. Themselves the primrose path of dalliance trod. And reeked not their own cede. I don't know whether these worthies suffered from corns, and they had been the week before cutting or paring them on the "wrong day." There is an old rhyme in connection with chiropody which says:— Cat them on Friday, cut them for woe; Cut them the next day a journey to go; Out them on Sunday, you cu., them for evil; For all the next week you'll be ruled by the Devil. I fancy the two individuals alluded to must have fallen completely and hopelessly under the influence of the Prin- ter's Devil when the one set up and the other passed the following sentence :—" Lord Rosebery presented a Bill for the Better Production of Young Girls, and it having been , read a first time, the House adjourned." I should think it did. When the copy of the Eirntinghant Daily Post (that ' of Friday, June 1) containing the astounding announcement reached me at the seaside village whither I had gone for a few days' holiday, I had just come in from a long walk through the cornfields and home by the seashore; and I at , once, after reading the marked sentence, adjourned to the kitchen to ask my landlady to brew me a strong cup of Lewis's tea, just to steady my nerves like. (Yes, lady readers, I confess to the weakneart of liking to indulge in a strong cup of the "wink-tipping cordial" in the afternoon.) My companion went so badly " off " over the little joke of ' the Birmingham printers that I bad to " lace " his " cup " Li with a dash of something stronger than lacteal fluid. Lord Rosebery is considered "clever" by those who know him • well; for instance, it is said that he peruses the literar lucubrations of his political opponents, and ponders his re- plies ttereto. while he is shaving himself. It is also affirmed that his lordship specially delights in reading the Duke of • Argyle's magazine articles while barbing. These are facts • of skill and acumen few men could perform. I have done duty at sales of yearlings, which the Earl has also attended with the view of adding to his stud, and the ' pleasure of a "pull " at the usual tankard of delightfully cool claret or champagne-cup passed round on a hot summer's day has been considerably enhanced by the • sight of his comely and cheery face, or the cheers that have followed his spirited biddings for a likely-looking colt or filly; and however much he may interest himself ,in improving the breed of race-horses, I do not think that lie is the kind of man that would in the same connection try his 'prentice hand on the human ;ace. The kind of thing imputed by the "Birmingham Primroses" to his lordship , could only be seriously entertained by persons of the same r I persuasion as the disciple of Bradlaugh and Besant who 11 the other day in a joursal of the irrational reformer order ' took upon himself to show, or attempted to show, how the chewing and digestive organs of the cow could be improved upon. The poor bull was left out of the question. Besides, , the character and conduct of the majority of English girls of the present day. are nearly a!l that could be desired. , What with schools for cookery and needlework, and the spread of a love for music, the younger female members of ' the family help to make the homes of the artisan class much more bright and attractive than they used to be. If a dis- ordered liver or a love-quarrel had anything to do with the confusion of the Birmingham compositor and reader, I • would, in conclusion, remind them of the old saw, which , tells us that L s' Green is forsaken, and yellow forsworn, But blue is the sweetest that ever was worn." And a blue pill and mental reflection in the open air under , the blue sky will very soon not only disperse the "green ' and yellow bile." but send the "green-eyed monster" to , the right-about. Blue is not only the "lucky sky-colour " ; it was also the sacred colour of the Druids, in Christianity it is the colour of the Virgin, and it is the colour of the short garment worn by the monster which, according to the Chineee mythology, specially delights in strangling devils of all kinds. What a blessing it would be if the C.M. could be induced to tear the hem off the tail of its shirt and strangle the P.D. with it. The women are very well as they are (God bless them !), while they are plentiful enough to supply good wives to all existing bachelors; and consider- ing that we owe their existence on•earth to the fact that un- grateful man deprived them of their wings when they first • descended from the clouds to nurse him in his dire ex- tremity, it is just corning it a little bit too strong—even from the point of view of a couple of bilious or disappointed Cax- , tonians who have allowed themselves to come under the influence of the P.D.—to suggest, let alone assert, that a Scotch nobleman, of all people in the world, should " pre- • sent a bill for their bette; production," and that the mem- bers of the House of Lords should have the p itience to read it. P.S.—ln the preface to "Zadkiel's Almanack " for 1883, Zadkiel Tao Sze says:—" In oar edition for 1881 we fore- told that the Eastern Question would write the future his tory of Europe in letters of blood and flame,' and that the 'British Navy would be engaged in many a battle.' In the , last edition we have said that about Midsummer there will , be great expenditure on munitions of war,' and that the effects of the recent Solar Eclipse would now be witnessed . in Egypt.'" If he had likewise, and at the same time, fore- told that a party of the printers employed on the almanack, while out enjoying their annual "beanfeast," would have , been caught in the heavy rainstorm of the 14th inst., while walking from Gadshill to Rochester, anti that they would , have to take refuge from the elements in some "black " , vehicles just disengaged from attending a funeral, he would have given a unique ocular proof of hi a ability to prophesy very correctly. When the funeral coaches alluded to pulled tip at a well-known inn in Rochester immortalised by Dickens, and discharged the beanfeasters in holiday attire , who occupied them, considerable astonishment was crested among the bystanders; but when the doors Of the very hearse aself swum,: open, and there emerged from the " Shillyheare " receptacle half-a-dozen jolly-looking minters (one of them a very fat man with bright and curly red hair, another about as long and thin "as they make them the crowd and the inn people were convulsed with laughter. Only "the little man in black" and the Printer's Devil, uniting forces, could have created such a situation. Talk of Dickens and the characters and scenes he conceived while walking to and fro between Gadshill and Rochester, after this! Truth is, indeed, stranger than fiction !!—A.S.
Why is a member of Parliament like a shrimp? Because he has M.P. at the end of his name.

"A WORD AND A BLOW !"—First Gent (Celt) : "Ye met 'm at me Brother's, the Mimber, I think ?"—Second Gent (Saxon) : "Yes, but I haven't any favourable impression of him—'n fact—urn—he struck me as a Liar. '—Virst Gent: "Did he, thin !? I hope ye Hit 'm back, Surr !" Punch.

A soldier in a newly-raised Irish corps observed to his comrade that a corporal was to be dismissed the regiment. "Faith and indeed," replied the other, "I hope it is the cor- poral so troublesome in our company." "What's his name ?- inquired the soldier. "Why, corporal punishment, honey, to be sure." The captain of an ocean steamer lately served out to the crew some of the cabin roast beef. The crew sent a man to the captain in remonstrance. The captain tasted the meat, and finding it all right, demanded the cause of the com- plaint. "Well, sir," said the spokesman, shifting his quid, "we don't like it; there ain't no chaw in it, sir." LOVE.—Love, how softly it speaks, loud enough though for the heart to hear. Love, that sacrifices nothing and suffers not—is not love. True love, thou rashest into tbe lap of God, from the heart. Love, thine accent is a sound from the heavenly kingdom of light. Love, thou art earnest, and happy, and enduring,andactive. Love pays everything, and remains n evert!' eless alwaysa debtor. Love, thy silenc eis beautiful, and far more lovely oft times thy speech. Love en- joys in self-denial, in action, in suffering for others. Love, thy strength is gentle, although of ten all-powerful. What love unites no fate can ever separate. Love, thou wilt one day unite all true lovers.

AUDUBON'S WIFE —Audubon, our great naturalist, married a good, sweet woman; and, when she began to find him out, she found he would wander off a thousand miles in quest of a bird. She said, "Amen !" and went with him, camped in the woods, lived in log hats and shanties on the frontier, anywhere to be with him. She entered into his enthusiasm, shared his labour, and counted all things but loss for the excellency Of the glory of being Audubon's wife. When the children began to come to them, he had to wander off alone; but he could not go into a valley so deep, or a wilderness so distant, that the light would not shine on him out of their windows. He knew exactly where he could find her, and how she would look ; for while, as Ruskin reminds us, the clouds are never twice alike, the sunshine is always familiar' and it was sun- shine he saw when he looked homeward. So, if you have read his notes, you will remember how his heart breaks forth into singing in all sorts of unexpected places, as he thinks of the wife and children waiting his return; and in that way they lived their life until they dropped into the lap cf God like mellow fruit.

FOREIGN INTELLIGOOE. CETEWAYO AND ZULULAND. Intelligence from Zululand announcing Usibepu,s. ack upon Cetewayo and the defeat of the latter is confirnaeo. Cetewayo, although wounded, succeeded in escaping. An immense number of his men were killed. A despatch from Capetown, dated abut three weeks ago, says the British President in Zululand had given emphatic testimony in f.tvour of the peaceable and loyal conduct of Cetewayo. Lord DerLy, in a letter to the Aborigines Protection Society, says he is not prepared to re-open the question of the partition of Zululand. The boundaries of Cetewayo's country have been fixed in strict accordance with the an- nouncement made to Cetewayo before his return and with the obligations of Her Majesty's Government to the chiefs placed over divisions of Zululand. . _
- A Durban telegram, dated Thursday, says :—The death of Cetewayo is fully confirmed. The Zulu King, all his wives, and many chiefs were killed. Usibepu has been every- where victorious.
The Aineer o f Afghanistan has formally signified to Lord Ripon's Government his acceptance of the offer of an annual subsidy.

The Earl of Derby has received a telegram from the Trans- vaal Volksraad stating that Mr. Paul Kruger, President of the Transvaal Government, will arrive in London to repre- sent Volksraad early in September. RIVER DISASTER IN AMERICA: 70 LIVES Losr.—While a number of excursionists from Battimore were standing on a pier on the Palapsco River on Monday evening, waiting for a barge which was to convey them home, the barge struck the end of the pier, which gave way and fell into the water, carrying with it a large number of people. Between GO and 70 persons were drowned, most of them being women and children.

A resume of the opinions expressed by the more impor- tant Paris journals with regard to the Suez Canal question shows they regard the withdrawal of the Convention with indifference, and praise the attitude of Mr. Gladstone in the face of the opposition which his proposals encountered. The essential fact, in their opinion, seems to be the acknow- ledgment which the English Premier made with regard to the legal position of M. de Lessens. TORNADOES IN AMERICA: A TRAIN OVERTURNED.— Severe tornadoes passed over Minnesota and Dakota on Monday. A railway train was overturned on the Chicago and North-Western R rilway by the force of the wind, and thirty-four of the passengers were injured. In another part three people were kind and several hurt through accidents caused by the violence of the tornado. It is further reported that nine people have been killed and fifty injured near Huron, Dakota. THE STRIKE OF TELEGRAPHISTS IN PHILADELPHIA.— The Times correspondent at Philadelphia reports that the conviction is becoming strenger that the telegraph companies will make some concessions to the men on strike. The only obstacle to a compromise, it appears, is the determination on the part of the companies not to recognise the Operators' Trade Union. The Western Union Company and the Baltimore and Ohio Company are reported to be already negotiating with the strikers. The telegraphic service is so badly crippled that the newspapers generally demand a speedy settlement of the dispute. The Western Union Co. is said to be losing 8100,000 daily. THE PANAMA. CANAL.—In a Parliamentary paper issued on Monday evening, containing consular reports on subjects of commercial and general interest, is a report by Acting. Consul Chamberlaine on the progress of the Panama Canal works. The consul mentions that Colon has been radically changed by the presence of the Interoceanic Canal Com- pany. It has risen from a small town of about 1,000 inhabi- tants to a busy place counting 10,000 souls. Traffic has greatly increased, and imports have assumed great propor- tions. There are 2,800 men at work for the company in Colon. When the whole line of canal is in full working order, there will be 800 locomotives, 10,000 waggons, and 200 excavators in use along the route. THE TAMATAVE INCIDENT.—The Paris correspondent of the Times writes that there is every appearance of the Tamativa incident having been greatly exaggerated and of its easy settlement. There is evidence, he adds, that no urgent or difficult qnestion exists between the English and French Governments, and that during the last fortnight there has been a change of tone in Paris calculated to allay all acrimony. A Berlin correspondent telegraphs that, ac- cording to private telegrams from London, the Tamative incident may be considered as ended. The English and French Cabinets are reported now to " acknowledge their mutual misunderstandings, and have agreed in an amicable spirit to say no more about the affair." THE SHAH OF PERSIA.—The Shah has left Teheran with a miscellaneous retinue, numbering, it is supposed, 10,C00, on what is said to be a pilgrimage to the shrine of the Imaun Rize at Meshed. -But that his Majesty should he accompanied in a pilgrimege by 3,000 horsemen, 2 000 in- fantry, and a body of gunners in charge of two field batter- ies, in addition to four or five thousand courtiers, attend- ants, and servants, raises some doubt as to the purely religious or ceremonial character of the journey. The dis- tance to be traversed is about 600 miles, and the Royal suite are provided with tents and other necessaries for the journey, while supplies of provisions have been collected at various points along the Boyal route. Why this imposing demonstration should be made in the North-Eastern corner of Persia, near to the frontiers of Afghanistan, and close to the country of the Tekke Turcomans, is a problem that has yet to be solved.

SWISS LABOUR STATISTICS.—The most recent report of the Department of the Interior states that there are in Switzerland 8,642 factories and workshops under legal super- vision, 1,472 of which are worked by machine power. Of these, water furnishes the movement to the amount of 41,316 horse-power, steam to the amount of 18,064, and gas to the amount of 117. The number.of operatives employed are 134,862, of which 70,364 are males and 64,498 females. There are 10,462 children between 14 and 16 years of age, 14,590 between 16 and 18, and 109,810 over the latter age. The textiles, such as cotton, silk, woollen, and linen, occupy 1,619 factories, with 85,70:5 workpeople ; 68 establishments carry on tanning, leather dressing, hair weaving, atc., with 3,753 hands; there are 6,636 hands employed in 143 food- preparing shops; 2,749 in 102 chemical works; 4,950 in 150 printing shops. There are also 111 wood-working establishments, occupying 2.913 hands; 353 for clock and jewellery making, with 24,988 workpeople ; and 96 for glass- making, &c., with 3,170. NEW GUINEA.—The despatch of the Earl of Derby to the Queensland Government on the proposal to annex New Guinea, and other correspondence on the same matter, has been issued. His Lordship says that Her Majesty's Govern- ment have not been able to approve the proceedings of the Colonial Government. It was well understood that any such extension of authority by colonial officers might lead to difficulties and complications. With a huge territory, and many social questions demanding attention, the Govern- ment of Queensland should not attempt the annexation of an island containiag several millions of savage inhabitants, who had not been shown to be anxious for civilized rule. In the absence of exceptionally strong reasons justifying the annexation, therefore, the home Government cannot sanction the proceeding.—A telegram from Melbourne says the movement in favour of the annexation of New Guinea and the New Hebrides gains strength throughout the Aus- tralian colonies. It will receive an additional impetus from the reports published in Melbourne of an "agitation" in New Caledonia for the annexation of the New Hebrides to the existing possessions of France.

FRANCE AND THE TONQUIN DISPUTE.—M. Challemel- Lacour has made a tolerably explicit statement in the French Senate as to the relations between France, China, and Anal!' in reference to the Toncinin dispute. Replying to the Due de Broglie, he said that war had not been de- clared against Anam by the French Government, nor by Tu Due against France, and no thought was at present enter- tained of establishing a blockade, though if any Power was found to be furuishine-' the Anamites with arms and ammu- nition, that step might be taken. All that France desires is, we are told, to cause her establishment in Tonquin to be re- spected, and to prevent Chinese and Anam marauders from committing outrages on French subjects. It is not believed that Tu Due had asked the assistance of China, and a deci- ded state of war does not prevail but it is added that the Paris Government is determined if it be found necessary to engage in hostilities against China in order to re-establish their authority in Tonquin, add resolutions to that effect are to be submitted to the Chambers. Revenge is meantime to be taken for the insults offered to the arms of France and the outrages perpetrated on her soldiers, while they will simultaneously suppress tumultous movements.

div.head: TFIE WESLEYAN CONFERENCE.
div.p: TFIE WESLEYAN CONFERENCE.

The one hundred and fortieth annual conference of the Wesleyan Methodist connexion commenced on Tuesday at- Hull. The retiring president, the Rev. Chas. Garrett, opened the proceedings, in which some 800 ministers took part. The voting for president resulted in the election of the. Rev. T. M'Cullagh, who received over 200 votes, and the Rev: R. N. Young was re-elected secretary. Mr. M'Cullagh's career strikingly illustrates the very varied experience which a Wesleyan minister necessarily requires under the. circuit system of that church. A native of Ulster, his first appointment was at Workington, after which be went to. Hexha n, then to Shotley Bridge and Consett. near New- castle, and next to Bishop Auckland. Having thus become familiar with the thoughts and feelings of the people of the extreme North, Mr. M'Cullagh was moved to London, and, after several years spent amongst the people of Spital- fields and the City-road, he was in succession stationed at Stockport, Sheffield, Lambeth, Liverpool, and Hull, and in 1882 he again returned to Liverpool. Among the circuit memorials presented to the Wesleyan Conference on Wednesday was one asking the Conference to "protest against vaccination as a sin against God." The memorial was laid aside. The question a where neat year's Conferense should be held gave rise to a somewhat excited discussion. There were three proposals, one in favour of Burslem, one for Nwca.stle-on-Tyne, and the third for post- poning the question to the Representative or mixed Con- ference. Eventually it was resolved, by a large majority, to hold the Conference in Burslem.

The Conference resumed on Thursday, the first business being the examinatkm of ministerial charater. This occu- pied a considerable time. Five ministers were reported to have resigned, one, the Rev. Jaceb Stevonson, taking excep- tm to the legislation at the last confe,rance regarding hap- tismal service for infants.

The q The Rochester Bridge-wardeuS nave resolved, with the his age on l'ioinelafy, sanction of the Charity Commissioners, to spend £20.000 of their surplus funds for educational purposes in Maidstone and Rochester. The mortality in 23 01 the largent Eteglieh towns during last week ranged from 127 per thousand per annum in Brighton to 2fl 'f in Newcastle-en-Tyne, the rate for Liver- pool behaeg 226. In the High Court of justiciary, FAinburgh, on Taesday, Lord Moncrieff passed a sentence of Tour months' imprison- ment on the ten4nen found guilty of participation in the Sabbatarian riot at Strome Ferry. Earl Granville presided at the annual meeting of the London Liberal Club, on Tuesday, and in an address to the members referred to the friendly character of our relations with other great Powers, especially emphasising the fact of the good understanding at present existing between this country and France. A frightful accident occurred in Sheffield on Tuesday. A slater, known only as Bill, from Birkenhead, in the employ of Messrs. Ellis and Wetherill, was lathing on the roof of the Britannia Music Hall, when he slipped off and fell into a yard below—a distance of 35 feet. He was fearfully in- jured. His recovery is doubtful. THE BISHOP or MANCHESTER.—Speaking at a luncheon held after the consecration of a new church at Preston, on Monday, the Bishop of Manchester said he had been bishop of the diocese for nearly 14 years, and he found his health failing. He yearned for the time when he should hand over the duties of his office to a younger man. LIBELLING A CLERGYMAN.—In the action at the Chester Assizes by the Rev. Thomas Price, of Prestatyn, against the , Rhyl Journal, for libel, a verdict was taken by consent for 405., coupled with an apology for the libellous abservations. , The Judge expressed his approval of the arrangement which had been arrived at. saying it was calculated to preserve the respect and esteem in which the Press of this country was generally held. BILLS OF SALE AND FAILURES. In the week ending July 21, 1883, there were 225 bills of sale in England and Wales, a decrease of 696 over those of the corresponding period last year; and the failures gazetted numbered 188, a decrease of 18. Totals for the portion of year to July 21, 1883, are—bills of sale registered for England and Wales, 6,941, a decrease of 20,591; the failures gazetted number 6,072, a decreaee of 167.—Stabb's Weekly Gazette. THE AGAR-ELLIS APPEAL CASE. In the Court of Appeal, on Tuesday, judgment was given in the appeal by the Hon. Mrs. Agar-Ellis and her daughter against the re- fusal of Mr. Justice Pearson to allow the daughter to spend her forthcoming holidays with her mother. The dispute arose s'me time back as to the education of the children Mr. Agar-Ellis being a Protestant and his wife a Roman Catholic, and it was then held that the father had a legal right to the custody of the children. The appeal was dis- missed. THE PRINCE OF WALES AND WESLEYANS.—The memorial stone of a new Wesleyan Chapel has just been laid at Englishbatch, near Bath, on land belonging to the Somerset portion of the Duchy of Cornwall, an excellent site having been leased by the Prince of Wales on merely nominal terms. Mr. W. Stoate, of Watchet, in laying the stone, said be questioned whether the ceremony of that kind had ever taken place under such favourable anspices. He thought the gift of the land by the Prince of Wales should lay them under an additional obligation of loyalty to the Queen and Royal Family. Other speakers also expressed their grati- tude to his Royal Highness. SINGULAR CHASE AFTER THIEVES.—On Tuesday morn- ing, shortly after one o'clock, a watchman named Cocker saw two men scale a wall bounding the iron foundry yard of Mr. H. Brooke, Colne-road, Huddersfield, and went in search of a policeman. Having found one, the two then roused the yard foreman of Mr. Brooke and proceeded to the foundary.l There they saw the Iwo men making their escape in thel direction of the river Colne. Being pursued, the men took 11 to the water and waded through, the officer and watchman following. When the latter got to the middle of the stream' the two men on the bank began to stone them. The officer held on his way, and he and the watchman chased the men, but they managed to escape. On going back it was found that the office door was prized open and the medium-sized office safe carried from its frame int.) the yard, where it had been deposited on an iron handbarrow ready for removal. The men burnt a number of office papers. • SINGULAR FAILURE or JUSTICE. The new rule as to gaol deliveries by judges of assize was the cause on Tuesday, at the Manchester Assizes, of a singular failure of justice, and Mary Ward was brought up as an hicorrigible rogue and vagabond from Rochdale' the magistrates there having committed her to the assizes for trial in obedience to the Home Secretary's order that all serious cases should be sent to the assizes in the event of their being held before the sessions. In this case it was pointed out that the statute provided that it should be dealt with at quarter sessions, aad that the magistrates ought, in spite of the Home Secre- tary's order, to have sent it to the sessions. It was suggested that as the judges were also justices for the county by reason of the commission, they might deal with it in that capacity, but Mr. Commissioner West, before whom the case came, said that even then one justice could not deal with it. Mr. West, having consulted Justices Stephen and Pearson, decided that he had no jurisdiction, and the prisoner was discharged. THE MANCHESTER CORPORATION MANURE. —ln January last, at a meeting of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society, held in Liverpool, Mr. A. Smetham, the society's analytical chemist, in the course of a lecture spoke disparagingly of the manure manufactured and sold by the Health Committee of the Manchester Corporation. The subjoined communication, from which it will be seen that the injurious statements are completely withdrawn, has recently been received from Mr. Smetham :—" Laboratory, Cereal Chambers, 18, Brunswick- street, Liverpool, June 22, 1833.—The Manchester Corpora- tion having taken exception to certain expressions in my lecture of the 29th January, 1883, in reference to the Man- chester Corporatien manure, I withdraw the same from my published pamphlet. Having been asked to withdraw my statement in relation to the Manchester Corporation manure, I have no hesitation in saying that I find franca recent analyses that the composition of the manure is in accordance with the analyses published ny the Corporation, and that it is a valuable artic'e.—ALFßED SIIETHAIL" LORD RIPON'S INDIAN POLIcY.—A numerously attended meeting was held on Monday night in the Memorial Hall, Farringdon-street, London, in support of Lord Ripon's Indian policy and Mr. Ilbert's Bill. Sir John B. Phear, who presided, was supported by Professor Thorold Rogers, Sir Wilfrid Lawson, Mr. J. Bryce, and many other members of Parliament. Letters approving Lord Ripon's policy were received from the Duke of Argyll, Lord Northbrook, Lord Lawrence and Earl Camperdown. The Chairman said that all who had experience of Indian affairs were of opinion that a large share of local self government should be given to the natives of India, and the only matter of dispute was the way in which it should be carried into effect. He be- lieved that Mr. Ilbert's Bill would obviate very great ad- ministrative inconvenience, and more firmly establish the eaprit de corps which should exist between European and native members of the civil service. Professor Thorold Rogers contended that a sense of Justice to India should prompt them to introduce such reforms as were necessary for the pacification and progress of the teeming millions of that empire. Sir Wilfrid Lawson described the Policy of Lord Ripon as praiseworthy and wise. They could not, he said, hope in future to hold India by the sword only, but would have to trust rather to the support of a liberal and en- lightened policy. Resolutions in support of the object of the meeting were unanimously passed. THE MACZONOCHIE CASE: SENTENCE OF DEPRIVATION. —The Dean of Arches gave judgment on Saturday in Vie suit against the Rev. A. H. Mackonochie. The question before his Lordship was whether the defehdiht ehould be' deprived of all ecclesiastical promotions in tire provitico of Canterbury. The defendant had been admonished by the Court of Arches repeatedly for his illegal Ritual let prat:, ices at St. Alban's, Holborn, and had treated its orders. with con- tempt, and had been ordered to be committed. Meantime an exchange of livings had been effected between Mr. Mackonochie and Mr. Suckling, incumbeet of St. Peter's, London Docks. The case was remitted to the Dean of Arches by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council for a "definitive sentence" to be passed, as his Lordship decided that he could not pass a perpetual inhibition, but only one of deprivation. Lord Penzance, after Mr. Mackonochie had been called and made no answer, read his judgment, which recapitulated the facts of the case, and defendant's continual contempt, and set forth the law on deprivation citing several instances in which the punishment had been awarded. His Lordship arrived at the conclusion that the offence had been fully proved, and he decreed the depriva- tion of the defendant from all his ecclesiastical promotions in the province of Canterbury, which included his present living of St. Peter's, London Docks. The defendant was also condemned in the costs. TIER RECENT ESCAPE OF THE IRISH MAIL—It may be remembered that recently Lord Sudeley, in the House of Lords, and Mr. Chamberlain, in the House of Commons, in reply to questions respecting the delay of the Irish mail through the driver and stoker of an engine having felien asleep on the London and North-Western Railway, stated that the driver had misrepresented the time he had been on duty, or he would not have been allowed to proceed. On Saturday, Mr. F. Harford, the general secretary of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants, received a letter from the driver, which shows that the man had been actually en duty 20t hours instead of 161- hours, as stated by the officials. The letter, which is dated from 13, Cecil- terrace, Chester, is as follows :—" Sir,—l hope you will ex- cuse me taking the liberty of writing to you. lam the driver of the light engine who fell asleep between Colwyn and Llandudno, and, as my case has been misstated in the papers, I wish to send you a true version of the facts. I commenced duty on June 26th at eight a.m, in the shed as extra engine- man. There came an order for a special to Cernarvon at 12.45, and I being there was sent with the train. I booked off the following morning at 430 a.m. Now, I wish you to understand that when we come into the shed as extra raen we are liable to be sent out at any moment. Shed time is not counted as on-duty time with a train, and when we go out with a train our time is only from when we start un- til we finish with the train. This order was issued by our foreman at Chester, and placed on the notice-board for all men to see, but it has been taken away since my misfortone. As regards my making a mis-statement as to the hours I had been on duty, I wish to clear myself on this imputation, for it is an understood thing when we are asked how long we have been on duty that it means out with the train, and I distinctly told the officials at Carnarvon and Chester the time I started with the train.--I remain, yours, RALPH CATHERALL."

VICAR'S REBUSE.—Preaching on Slinday tight, the vicar of Stratford-on-Avon made a most extraordinary statement. He said the behaviour of young girls and young men who sat in the south gallery of the church was at times SO reprehensible that he dreaded to see any respectable vir- tuous girl go there. It was a great scandal, and he hoped the churchwardens would separate the sexes, as was done tt.lnany other churches. THE FLIGHT OF THE BOOTLE TOWN CLERK. It is !said that Pierce, the defaulting town clerk at Bootle, in Order to accomplish his frauds, already found to amount to neatly £23,300, had recourse to a most artful device, in ad- to committing forgery. The corporate seal was kept in a box which could only be opened—legitimately opened at least—by means of two keys of different construction, one held by the mayor and the other by the towu clerk; and it has been discovered that Pierce had somehow got temporarer Possession of the mayor's key, argl had a duplicate made. The Bolton magistrates on Monday committed a man named Dugdale to prison for three months on a conviction ler offering diseased meat for sale. Even in the records of the repulsive "bad meat" trade such an offence as that brought home to Dugdale is rare. Being in possession of a diseased cow, which was, by magisterial order, killed and buried, the defendant at night exhumed the carcase and was removing it to Bolton when interrupted by the police. A regard for the public health prompts one to echo the com- Plaint which was heard from the bench—that under the statute Dugdale's imprisonment will be without hard labour. Mr. Smith was born at Ogbourne St. George, near Marl- borough, on July 21, 1783. He spent most of his life in his native county, and he has for 13 years resided with his B°O, Mr. Robert Smith, at Holm Pierrepent. In the early days of his life he spent much time on horsebick, and his health is still very good. Thirty years ago he discarded spectacles as realer a hindrance than a help to his sight, and he now reads without their aid. ALLEGED PERJURY BY A MINISTER.—At Birmingham, on Monday, Thomas Llewelyn Osgyinry, the pastor of a Welsh Wesleyan congregation worshipping in 'Vfasshouse- lane, was charged with committing perjury by swearing in the county court that he had not put his signature to an agreement regarding the rent of a house he had resided in belonging to Mr. Frank Taylor. an accountant. The prose- cution was at the instance of the Treasury. Evidence was given by Mr. Taylor and his clerk that the prisoner put his signature to the agreement, and other evidence proved that the prisoner swore in the county court that the Signature was a forgery. ALARMING GAS EXPLOSION IN A CHAPEL.—On Sunday eVening a gas explosion occurred at the United Methodist Free Church, Galley Wall-road, Bermondsey. Just before the time for commencing service, and wl.ile the congrega- tion were assembling, Mr. Fender, an official, noticed a arnell of gas proceeding from one of the vestries. He went in to examine the gas pipes, and incautiously struck a light •to test them. An explosion immediately took place, which - shattered the glass in the building, and the vestry, which contained a quantity of loose paper banners and other in- flammable material, was set on fire. Mr. Pander ran out in a scorched condition, and the congregation, amid the shrieks and cries of the women and children, leaped over the seats and rushed towards the doors. The Rev. T. Kench, the Minister, and the officials at once set to work to put out the flames, aud with the aid of a plentiful supply of water sue- ?eeded. It was then found that there was a defect in a pint of one of the gaspipes running along the ceiling. It Was with difficulty that the minister could prevail upon ula congregation to re-enter, but this was ultimately accomplished, and the service proceeded without further interruption. THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES.—Business generally in the iron trade of this district continues want- ing in animation. The inquiry for pig iron is extremely small. For Lancashire pig iron moderate offers ate reported at 3d to 6d under quoted prices. These, however, are de- clined, as makers are fairly wail sold for the remaiuder of the year, and at the full rates there is very little being done. District brands of pig iron meet with very little inquiry, but quoted prices are nominally nrichenged. Finished iron makers are kept fairly well supplied with orders, and are firm in their prices. No great weight of business is dfering, but orders come steadily forward for bars and hoops, whilst for sheets there is a brisk demand, stimulated to some extent by the continued stoppage of many of the Staffordshire sheet mills. For sheets delivered equal to Manchester or Liverpool local makers have no difficulty in realising £8 per ton; hoops are quoted at £6 12s 63, with good specifications taken at a little less; and bars at £6 5s per ton. The ship- ping trade continues only moderate. Any definite action with regard to the reduction of wages in this district is still held in abeyance pending the final settlement of affairs in Staffordshire, and the men at the Lancashire forges con- tinue working at the old rates.—For the time of the year there is generally a fairly good demand throughout the coal trade of the district, and although business is still quiet the summer season is being got through more satisfactorily than has been the case for several years past. The pits are work- ing better time—four and in some cases five days a week— end although in the district round Manchester stocks have at some of the collieries been accumulating heavily, there is not generally throughout Lancashire any very large weight of coal put down on the pit banks. Prices are also very well maintained, and it is only for quantities where buyers are able to clear off quickly accumulations of stock in waggons that any material concessions are made. In the market generally rather more animation has been shown dur- ing the past week; house-fire coals have been going off rather more freely, and there has been a good demand for shipment, which has helped to move away the common-- classes of round coal. Herne-trade requirements are with- out much change, and common slack still hangs in the market. At the pit mouth prices remain about as finder:— Best coal, 9s; seconds, 75, common round coal, 5s 6il to Go; burgy, 4s 6d to ss; good slack, 4s to 4s 3d; and common sorts, 3s to 3s 31 per ton. For shipment steam coal averages 7e 3d to 7s 6d ; and seconds house coal 8s 6el per ton delivered at Crarston and Liverpool.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—TITURSDAY. In the course of a short conversation which Lord Laming ton raised as to the Euphrates Valley railway project, the Marquis cii SALISBURY said he did not wish to press the par- ticuler matter of the Euphrates Valley line upon the Go- vemment,but he hoped they were not to consider the subject of increased facility of communication between the Medi- terranean and Indian Ocean as entirely closed: but that before the session finished they would have an intimation from the Government of the definite policy they were pre- pared to follow in respect of it. The Companies (Colonial Registers Bill was read a second time. The Prison Service (Ireland) Bill also passed the second reading. The Con. mons' amendments to the Sea Fisheries Bill were considered and agreed to. The Companies Acts Amendment Bill and the Sea Fisheries (Ireland) Bill passed through committee. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY. WITCHCRAFr AND CANNIBALISM.--Mr. ASHLEY, replying to Mr. A. M'Arthur, said the Colonial Offica had received a despatch from the officer administering the Government of Sierra Leone repotting the burning in the Sherbro country of 34 persons who had confessed to witchcraft and canni- balism, but intimating that the chiefs had promised him to abstain from such practices in future. CHOLERA IN EGYPT.—In reply to Lord Folkestone, Lord HARTINGTON said so far as he knew there had been 14 cases of cholera among tie English troops in Egypt, and 11 had proved fatal. THE ORDER OP BUSINESS.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE asked for information as to the measures the Government were going to withdraw and as to the time of closing the session.—Mr. GLADSTONE, said the motion about the Suez Canal had deranged his calculations as to business, but full time would be given for the discussion of Supply. The Government di.d not expect to be able to proceed with the Detention in Hospitals Bill, the Criminal Law Bill, or the Welsh Educa- tion Bill, lie would give Monday for the discussion of the Suez Canal motion. With regard to the terms of the motion the Government entirely agreed with it, but did not con- template discussion as desirable till the trading and shipping interests of the country had considered the question in its various phases. The Government did not contemplate in any way any early negotiations of such a character as could possibly bear upon the Claims of M. de Lesseps and the Suez Canal Company, but they had 'a s'rong objection to the passing of any such resolution by the House from which they anticinated there might be public disadvantages, and therefore it would be their duty to sup- port the amendment of the hon. membn for Hull.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE mid his object was to retain for the House its freedom of judgment in a matter in which he was of opinion that its freedom was somewhat compromised by the p: o- ceedings of the Government. HE SUEZ CANAL.—Questions relating to the Suez Canal were again very numerous. Lord E. FazaiamacE ei- plained that communications regaring the abandoned pro- posals had been received from Rusia and Italy.—Baron de

them to pay their debts. Mr. Edward Harrington, brother of the member for Tip- perary and manager of the Kerry Sentinel newspaper, who was sentenced to six months' imprisonment for conniving at the printing of threatening notices, was arrested on Mon- day and conveyed to Tralee gaol. The Lord Lieutenant has informed the President of the Irish College of Physicians that he is "unable to consider that the bestowal of honours by the Crown can be made the subject of discussion between him and any public body; and while, therefore, entertaining great respect for those who addressed him, he must decline to discuss with them the question which they have brought under his notice." The fifteen men in custody on a charge of shooting Mrs. Smythe at the gate of her residence, Barbavilla House, West- meath, were on Tuesday committed for trial at Mullingar on the capital charge. A witness named Hanlon, who was for- merly in custody, supplemented the powerful circumstan- tial evidence by identifying three of the prisoners, whom he saw running away from the house after shots had been fired. An inquest has been held at Limerick on the bodies of four children who were found in a manure heap at the rear of an old house in Roches-street. the medical testimony showed that the children had been born alive, three of them being complete, while the other had been cut in pieces. Six months must have elapsed since death, and the remains were shockingly decomposed. An open verdict was returned. The monthly detailed return of the Land Commission shows that during April fair rents were fixed by the Sub- commissioners in 3,259 cases, involving a gross rental of £69,359, and an acreage of 99.776 acres. The aggregate judicial rent amounted to £55,432, the Poor Law valuation being L5l 256. The total reduction was, therefore, £13.917, or about 20 per cent. In Ulster the rents appear to have been reduced by about 224 per cent., while in Muneter they appear to have been lowered by only 13 per cent. News of an unpleasant kind has been received from Ire- land. It is not associated in this instance with sedition, assassination, or outrage, but its effect upon the people, if it should be true, will certainly be serious. It is well known that the population of the sister kingdom are largely depen- dent upon the potato crop, and that when affected by dis- ease the result is certainly distress, and frequently famine. Considerable uneasiness has been caused by a report that potato disease has made its appearance, and is spreading in West Cork, a district in which an abundant harvest of the crop had been calculated upon. It can only be hoped that the wasteful scourge will be confined to the fields in which it has already been discovered. THE CAREY FAMILY.—A fee, days ago the family of Peter Carey, the informer, suddenly left Beverley, where they had been staying with their relatives for more than a month. A Dublin detective arrived in the town for the pur- pose of protecting Mrs. Carey and her children, who were, it is said, in fear of annoyance, their whereabouts haying become known to those alleged to be on their track. The detective officer accompanied the family frenn Beverley to their destination, which was not known even to their friends. The Irish Times says: In consequence of the publication of several stories about James Carey being at present in London, or some other part of the United Kingdom, it may be well to state that the authorities have received a telegram announcing the safe arrival of himself and family on the previous day at h.§ colonial destination. THE LAND Coußvs.—The strictures passed by the HOLM of Lords Committee on i.he administration of the Land Act by the sub-commissioners has provoked a rejoinder from the Chairman of the County Kerry Commission, Mr. John George M'Carthy, formerly member for Mallow. In deliver- ing judgment in some cases at Calairciveen on Saturday, Mr. M'Carthy admitted that some of the charges were very serious, but, said he, "so far as this Commission is con- cerned they are absolutely without foundation." Rents were not fixed accordingto some juggle of arithmetical figures, as stated by the Lords Committee, for if way commis- sioners were "guilty of a fraud so reckless and so heartless they deserved not merely dismissal but impeachment. We interfere," Mr. M'Carthy proceeded, "with contract only to secure justice. If the contracted rent be fair, it is left unaltered; if it be toe low, it is increased ; if it be too high, it is reduced. All depends upon the facts of the case, the results of the inspection, and the law appli- cable to both. That redactions occur in the vast majority of cases is neither our fault nor our merit. We did not fix the rents, which no court of justice could honestly or legally: declare to be fair, or could deal with otherwise than by re- duction." Having stated that the work of his Commission was done with the utmost care, with straighforward impar- tiality towards all concerned, and with a single-minded desire to do justice, Mr. M'Carthy concluded with the re- mark that he and his brother Commissioners were incap- able of being turned aside from the straight path of duty by the clamour of either peasants or peers."

THE MINERS' DEMONSTRATION AT HAYDOCK PARK. The demonstration of miners, under the auspices of the Ashton and Haydock Miners' Trade Union, which will be held in Haydock Park this (Saturday) afternoon, promises to be very successful. It will be the first of its kind in the district, and it is to be hoped that fine weather will favour the gathering. Four brass bands have been engaged for the afternoon, and about noon will paraple the entire district. They will afterward meet on Ashton Heath, and after a pro- cession of the men has been formed will march through the principal streets a Ashton, an then to Haydock Park, which has been kindly lent by Dr. Beaman. Here a large open-air meeting will be held, and it is confidently antici- pated that oddresses on trade union questions will be given by Mr. Charles Bradlaugh, M.P., Mr. Burt, M.P., and several officials connected with the Miners' Organisation. A series of athletic sports will follow, and prizes amounting in valbte to £2l will be competed for.
MURDEROUS ASSAULT WITH A POKER .AT PRESCOT.

A middle-aged woman, named Mary Donnelly, was brought before Mr. W. L. Evans, at Prescot, on Thursday afternoon, charged with unlawfully wounding Catherine Mullern, by striking her on the head with a poker.—Prose- outrix stated that about half-past nine o'clock on Tuesday night, she was passing prisoner's house iu Mill-lane. Prescot, when prisoner, who was standing at the door, called her to her and asked why she had not come to help her with some mugs on the previous day. She replied quietly, but prisoner called her very foul names, an I seizing a poker dealt her two very severe blows, one on the left side of the head and the other on the forehead, knock- her down insensible. When she recovered consciousness she went to the police office bleeding profusely, and she was 1 taken to Dr. Hall's surgery, where her wounds were dressed by Dr. O'Hara.—Dr. O'Hara. stated that the wound on the side lof the head was a very severe one, about an inch in diameter, penetrating to the bone and severing an important artery. which bled very freely. The wound on the forehead peas also a very serious one although not so serious as the other. Had surgical assistance not been promptly obtained the woman would certainly have bled to death. She was in great danger for that (Tuesday) night, and even yet was not out of danger.—The prisoner was apprehended by P.C. Middlebrook and other officers at her own fieus.?. In answer ' to the charge she said she did not know she bad done it, ' but she might have done it in self defence.
