Worms questioned Mr. Gladstone as to M. de Lcssep's claim to a monopoly, but failed to indu .e the Premier to enter upon controversial matter; and Sr Henry Wolff, Mr. Gorst, M. Labouchere, and Mr. Chaplin were equtlly unsuccess- ful in their efforts to induce the Prime Minister to make in- convenient admissions. THE EDUCATION ESTIMATES.—The House went into Committee of Supply, and Mr. MUNDELLA. made his, annual statement on the Education Estimates. He said the vote of £2,938,930 for public education in England and Wales showed an increase of £146,945. The average atten- dance had increased in the year by 144,000, and to-day there were on the registers of the public elementary schools 4,33l,ooo,against 1,600,000 when the Education Act was passed. The number of children on the rolls of voluntary schools was 2,884,250, and on the rolls of Board schools 1,305,362. The accommodation for children had now reached 4,538,000 places. The most gratifying feature of the present report was the increase in the average atten- dance and in the upper standards. The right, hon. gentle- man unfortunately contrasted the position uf this country in educational matters with various Continental States, but said we had reached a time of increasing strength, and if we were only patient and persistent we should in another generation compare well with an other country.—Mr. S. SMITH called attention to the overworking of scholars and pupil teachers, and said that a number of deaths from brain fever had came to his knowledge during his inquiries into the subject. Ile urged the appointment of a select committee on the subject.—Sir LYON PLAYFAIR combated Mr. Smith's statements.—Mr. RICHARD and Mr. L. TANLEY drew attention to a grievance of Nonconformists in regard to certain Church of England training colleges.

THE STATE oF IRELAND. JAMES CAREY AND THE DUBLIN CORPORATION. The opinions of the Trish Attorney-General and the Solicitor-General upon the case submitted to them respect- ing James Carey's position in relation to the Dublin Corpo- ration have been sent in. The law officers point out that James Carey having been declared a bankrupt, his seat as ccruncillar for Trinity Ward is consequently vacated • and they advise the Corporation to issue a proclamation for an election in his stead. This consequently implies that the election of Dr. Wade was not legal. A committee of the whole House is to be summoned to consider the matter. DEATH OF MR D. M. O'CONOR, M.P. Mr. Dennis M. O'Conor, M.P. for Sligo County. who has been seriously ill for some time, died on Thursday morning at five o'clock at his residence at Queen's Gate, from con- gestion of the lungs. The deceased was the second son of the late Mr. Dennis O'Conor, the O'Conor Don (who repre- sented Roscommon from 1821 till 1847). Born in 1840, he was educated at Downside College, near Bath, and at Lon- don University, where be graduated M.A. in 1861, and had the honorary degree of LL.D. conferred upon him in 1666. In the last mentioned year he was called to the bar at the Middle Temple. A Liberal in politics, though in favour of Home Rule for Ireland, he was returned for the County of Sligo in December, 1868, and retained his seat for that constituency up to the time of his death.

CAPTAIN WEBB DROWNED AT NIAGARA.

Captain Matthew Webb has met a fate which will stir- price no one who knew of the perilous enterprise which he had undertaken. For a consideration amounting to 10,000 dole., subscribed by railway companies who hoped to profit by conveying excursionists to witness the performance, Webb undertook to swim through the whirlpools and rapids baow Niagara Falls. Fully warned of the danger, he made the venture on Tuesday and perished in the attempt. He left the Canada side of Niagara, below the falls, in a small boat, and rowed to a point about 300 yards above the old suspension bridge. He dived into the river at four o'clock in the afternoon, and on entering the rapids was almost turned over by the force of the water. Heiswans the rapids with great determination, being now and again caught sight of by a few of the spectators. When last seen be was enter- ing the whirlpool, and at first appeared to be doing well, but very shortly afterwards threw up his wins and disappeared. He was not seen again. Captain Webb will be principally remembered for his cele- brated swim across the Channel in 1875. He made an un- successful attempt on August 12th, but when he had got half way across he was compelled to desist, and was taken into the beat which accompanied him. On the 24th August he was more successful. He left Dover from the Admiralty Pier at a few minutes before one p.m. attended by a lugger and two rowing boats. He held on his course without a sign of weakness during the evening and night, and landed on the west side of Calais harbour a little after half-past ten in the morning, having remained in the water, without even touching a boat on the way, 211 hours. He was supplied from time to time with refreshments from the boats that ac- companied him—brandy, beef tea, and coffee—but no solid food passed his lips. The sea was calm till the French coast was nearly reached, when the flood tide set in and drifted Captain Webb eastward towards Calais. A breeze springing up, the sea ran high and broke over the boats, but the intrepid swimmer persevered, and at last touched ground. He was too weak te stand, but with assist- ance he walked ashore, and after a sleep felt none the worse for his unparalleled feat. Thursday's Sportsman, in a second edition, publishes a special telegram from its Toronto correspondent giving full details of the tragical death of Captain Webb. It stated that it was doubted up to the very last moment whether Webb would attempt the feat, but he arrived at the falls at one o'clock on Tuesday, and looked over the course. He started for the river at half-past three, and was rowed to the centre, the banks being crowded. He was fully composed, and seemed quite confident of success. He was warned by a ferryman not to proceed, but he laughed and did not answer. At two minutes past four he dived, and swam leisurely down the river. He passed along the rapids at a great rate but swimming with ease:ond confidence. He was soon:however, whirled along at a frightful pace, and was swept into tho neck of a whirlpool, where he was at the mercy of the furious eddies. He was then drawn under and seen no more. He is reported to have said that ha would not receive anything from the rail way companies if success- ul.

HORRIBLE FATALITY AT ITUYTON QUARRY. A PORTER Cur TO PIECES. On Saturday evening, Edwin James, a porter at Huyton Quarry station on the London and North-Western Railway, lost his life in a most horrible manner. He was crossing the line to attend to a slow train from Liverpool to Man- chester, when the express from Manchester to Liverpool, which was travelling at the rate of sixty miles an hour, and which he does not seem to have perceived, came up. The engine struck him on the head, completely shattering it, and bestrewing the line and platform, and even the windows of the station offices, with his brains and blood. His body was carried by the train a distance of 250 yards, and com- pletely dismembered, and in fact almost cut to pieces. The remains were collected in a sheet by P.C. Cameron, the sta- tion officials and others, one foot being picked up at some distance from the station, and carried to the Seel Arms. One foot with part of the leg was carried by the train to Lime- street, and from thence to Allerton, near Gersten, where it was discovered. Deceased, who was held in much respect, leaves a widow and four children, with whom much sym- pathy is felt. He had only been employed at the station about six months. The inquest was held on Tuesday, at the Seel Arms, Huvton Quarry before Mr. T. W. Barker. The police were represented by P.S. Edgar, and Mr. Ferrand and Inspector Peters attended on behalf of the railway cornpanv.—Eliza Jones, deceased's mother, stated tbat her son was 30 years of age, and resided at Blyth's cottages, Huyton Quarry.—Gcorge Bramhall, signalman at Huyton Quarry station, deposed that deceased had been a porter there about six months. He was porter one week and staff man the other. Witness was on duty in the signal box on Saturday evening, and saw the accident happen. The 5-5 express from Liverpool to Manchester bad just passed, and the five o'clock express from Manchester, which WAS due at Huyton Quarry about half-past five, was just coining down. It had been signalled, and deceased could have seen that the signals were off. Deceased was looking through the windows of the porter's room for a slow train on the north line, and just as witness was about to ring the bell for the slow traife deceased came out of the porters' room and stepped off the platform right in front of the express. He wou,d know that the express was due, but the abutment of the bridge might prevent him seeing it. His object in crossing the line was to attend to the slow train from Liverpool. He was in the habit of attending to the slow train and would know that the express was due. Sometimes he would wait till the express had passed before crossing the line, but sometimes if the express happened to be a little late he would ge over first. On this occasion the express was up to the minute. Deceased was struck down instantly. The train was travelling at about sixty miles an hour. It was his duty to have waited till the train passed, but he walked out of the porters' room looking right before him, and stepped in front of the train without looking to either right or left. He might have seen that the signals were off if he had looked. The express would be 100 yards from the station when witness put his hand on the bell to call the officials out to attend to the slow train, but as the express was so near he did not ring the bell. Deceased had no notice to cross the line, and he attempted to do so on his own responsibility. The stationmaster was in his room at the time. Deceased was a very steady man.—Mr. Ferrand stated that the driver and fireman of the express had been telegraphed for, but they could not come in time, and.they knew nothing except that the driver saw deceased just as he was struck by the engine —Eva Attwood, wife of James Attwood, Huyton Quarry, stated that she was on the platform intending to travel by the slow train to Manchester, and saw deceased come out of the porters' room underneath the steps leading up to the bridge. He jumped upon the line just in front of the express, and she saw him struck by the engine. She was so upset that she could not tell whether a bell was rung just before the ex- press arrived, but she thoueht not.—The Coroner, in sum- ming up, said the only thing which had struck him in the course of the evidence was that if the signalman had rung the bell to warn the porter to cross the line to attend to the other train when the express was due it would not have been a correct thing to have done, but he did not seem to have done so. He could not see that anyone was to blame. Probably deceased was too anxious to discharge his duties, and this terrible accident occurred.—The jury at once re- turned a verdict of "Accidental death," exonerating every- one from blame.—Mr. Ferrand stated that although de- ceased had only been in the service of the company six months his widow would be entitled to £BO by arrangement with the company. _

Reports were current on Thursd 4y. night that two cases of cholera had occurred in this country—one in Wales and the other in the London Docks. The Liverpool City Council are seeking power to prevent the importation of rags from Egypt. A more dangerous cargo than bundles of rags from a cholera-stricken country could scarcely be imagined. On Thursday, at the Oldham Police Court, summonses were granted against three barbers for having their shops open on Sunday. They were taken out under an Act passed in the reign of Charles the Second, which the clerk said was a dead letter law. The bench, whilst saying people must get shaved, assented to the summonses being granted. They are taken out at the instance of a Rairdressene Association which has adopted Sunday closing. George Henry Pym was on Vattraay sentenced, at the Nottingham Assizes, to we years' penal servitude for f ilsifying accounts, and zino,zzling the money of the Malle- able Iron Company. He had only been with the company 15 months and his accounts showed a deficiency to the amount of £l,OOO. The manager of the company, in answer to the judge, stated that the prisoner owed his posi-

tion to betting on horse races. Mary Kate Bailey, 10 years of age, was charged at Clitheroe, on Thursday, with attempting to commit suicide in the river Ribble the previous night. Prisoner several times climbed a wall to leap into the river, but was pre- vented by two operatives who had followed in suspecting her intention. Prisoner, who said she attempted to commit suicide in a fit of madness, and would have done so if she had not been prevented, was handid over to her relatives. A novel experiment, suggested by the aim of the Fisheries Exhibition and the protest against the monopoly of the fish profits existing in provincial towns, was made on Thurs- day morning by the Mayor of Stafford. At his own risk he ordered several tons of- fish direct from Grimsby, and an- nounced itto be sold at twopence per lb. in the fish market. As the average price of fish in Stafford is eightpence per lb., there was an enormous rush of people on Thursday morning to the fish market, the whole of it being sold in 40 minutes. The experiment is, it is said, to be repeated. ENGLISH PATENTS. - The following patents amongst others published in the Commissioners of Patents Journal were sealed during the week ending July 21st, 1883 Frederick Attock, Newton Heath, Manchester, improvements in or applicable to couplings of railway wagons and other vehicles running on rails; John Muir, Hetherington, Man- chester, machinist, improvements in revolving fiat carding engines; Benjamin Harlow, Macclesfield, improvements in steam boiler and other futnaces and fronts and doors there- for; James Watt Boulton. Ashton, engineer, improvements in or applicable to steam boilers or generators; Charles Henry Andrew, Stockport, engineer, improvements in lubri- cators particularly applicable to motor engises ; James iligham, Newton *Heath, improvements in knitting machines; Henry Southwelt, Heywood. and William Henry Dawson, Manchester, improvements in the construction of bobbies used for cotton and woollen spinning; Giles Atherton,Stock- port, hat manufacturer, improvaments in the finishing of hats—(a communication from abroad.)--List supplied by Mr. George Davies, CE, Fel. Inst. P.A., Patent Solicito:. 4, St, Ann's-square, Manchester.

ST. HELENS NEWS. THE Sr. HELENS INDEPENDENT CHAPEL.—The plans for the alterations of the Old Independent Chapel, St. Helens, having been decided upon by the special committee, tenders were invited for the cartying out of the work. At a meet- ing held on Tuesday night the tender of Messrs. George Harris and Son, contractors, Liverpool-road, St. Helens for £2,700 was accepted, and as the alterations are to be imme- diately commenced, the services will be conducted in the Town Hall early in August, and be continued there until the 'contract has been fulfilled. SACRED HEART SCHOOLS, Sr. HELENS —The following is the list of students who have successfully passed the ex- amination in inorganic chemistry,held in connection with the Bacre4 Heart Schools :—First-class: John B. C. Kershaw, and George Skeath. Second-class: Wm.. Holt, William Williamson, Charles F. Weatherilt, Hen y W. Roughley, Arthur Lackland, Arthur Richardson, James J. Macdonald. Ten students were examined, two obtaining first-class certi- ficates, and seven second-class certificates, only one failing to pass. Mr, Thomas Lyons' was the teacher of the class. ELECTION OF A TOWN HALL KEEPER FOR Sr. HELENS.— A good deal of interest is being taken in St. Helens regard- ing the appointment of a town ball keeper, with wife to assist, and no fewer than 213 applications have been received. On Ihnrsday the Parliamentary Committee were occupied'a considerable time in coneider ing these applica- tions, and eventually five persons were selected to appear before the committee to-day, when the name of the most suitable candidate will be entered upon the committee's minutes and recommended to the Council for appointment. TRINITY COLLEGE, LONDON: MRS. 1 HACKER'S MUSIC ACADEMY, Sr. HELENS.—The following is a list of Mrs. Thacker's candidates in the examinations in pianoforte playing in connection with Trinity College, London, Leld June 11 to 15, in the Philharmonic Hall, Liverpool, Mr. Humphrey J. Stark, Mn. Bac. Oxen., being the examiner. —Junior Division : Honours, Miss _alice H. Jackson ; special mention, Miss Louie Varley ; Mise Sarah Simms, Miss E. H. Taylor.—Prienene neaision : Pass, Miss Louie Houghton, Miss Adelaide K. Wood, and Miss Emma J. Johnson. FOOTRACE AT Sr. HELENS FOR £5O —Despite the con- tinuous downpour of rain, the sporting elementaof Helens mustered in strong force at the Recreation Grounds, on Saturday, to witness the 150-yard sprint between J. Kay and Bury's novice, the latter being better known as the "Post Boy." The stakes were £25 a side, Kay beingethe recipient of an inside start of one yard. The odds were 5 to 2on Kay, who gained an advantage at the start, and keeping in front the whole of the way won very easily by two yards. W. Wood, of Sutton, trained the winner, and the" Post Boy " was self-trained. SERIoUS RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT Sr. HELENS.—On Thursday afternoon a serious and painful accident happened , to a young man named Joseph Cunliffe, a shunter employed bY the London and North-Western Railway Company. leunliffe, it appears, had been engaged in shim-Ling "dine waggons on the Rayenhead branch line near Ravenhead, and when leaving a waggon unfortunately came in contact with the canal bridge. He fell, and it is said one of his arms and one leg were broken by the wageon. He was at once conveyed to the infirmary at Liverpool. The unfor- nate man is about 25 years of age, and lived with another railway employn, named Bradbury, at Sutton. ASSAULT BY Sr. HELENS COLLIERS AT BILLINGE.—At Wigan Police Court, on Monday, James Swift and John Moran, colliers, St. Helens, were charged with wounding Constable Hodgson, at Billinge, the previous night. It ap- neared that the constable, when passing a farm in the owe- ' pation of Mr. Heald,at Billinge.heard voices which attracted • hisattention. On goingto the place he found the prisoner and another man. One of the men had something in his pocket which the constable thought it righe to make inquiries about. The plisoners not liking the interference of the con- stable, thereupon set upon, kicked him savagely, and cut his head open.—They were remandea. Sr. THOMAS'S CRICKET Cavil, Sr. HELENS.—The mem- bers of this club gave a complimentary dinner to the mem- bers of the St. Saviour's (Liverpool) C,icket Club, in the Fleece Hotel, St. Helens, on Saturday last. The chair was occupied by Mr. W. Irving, captain, of t he St. Sayionl's ; and the vice-chair by Mr. C. Cousins, captain of St. Thomas's. In the course of the evening the usual toasts were proposed and honoured. and the success of both clubs heartily drunk. The evening was enlivened by a number of songs, and Mr. H. Ceiling, of Liverpool, rendered in a very humorous manner "The Irishman," " Birkenhead Eisteddfod," etc. The sioging of "Auld lang sync' brought a pleasant gathering to a close. MARRIAGE AT Sr. HELENS.—,On Wednesday morning a large number of persons, chiefly young ladies, assembled in the Congregational Chipel, St. Helens, to witness the mar- riage of Mr. James Sharpies, nephew of Mr. C Sharpies, draper, St. Helens, and Miss Annie Makin, Cooper-street. The Rev. R. J. Ward officiated. During the service a hymn was sung by the choir, and at the conclusion Mr. H. Knowles played the wedding mere!' on the organ. On leaving the chapel the newly united pair were saluted by a shower of rice, which continued to pour over them till they were safely ensconced in their carriage. In the afternoon they left 51. Helens for the lake district, whete they intend to spend the honeymoon. THE LAW OF BICYCLING.—At Prescon on Tuesday, Jas. Ball, a traveller, and Wm. Appleton, an engine driver, of t. Helens, were convicted of riding their bicycles on the big, st- way after sunset without lighted lamps. The offence was committed at nine o'clock on the evening of the 4th inst., and the defendants pleaded that on their way from Liverpool they were detained by a thunderstorm, that they had lamps, but had neglected to trim them, hoping to reach St. Helens , before dusk, and that their impression was that they were not required to light their lamps till 'dusk, and that it was daylight when they passed through Prescot, and were stopped by P.S. Poßtt.—Mr. Willis pointed out that the law required the lamps to be lighted _after sunset, and that bicyclists should ascertain the law before they began to ride. —The magistrates admonished the defendants and dismissed them on payment of 6d. and 48. 6d. costs, one of the defen- dants in retiring, remarking that he would know the law better in future. INTERFERING WITH A CORPORATION EMPLOYE. Two men named Thomas Kerfoot and James Dickson were, on Monday, charged at the St. Helens Police Court with havicg wilfully damaged a lamp, the property of the M ,yor alder- men, and burgesses of St. Helens, at Parr, on the 12th and also with having obstructed John Doyle, a nightsoil- man employed by the Corporatioo, whilst in the execution of his duty.—lt was statec by Doyle that on the night in question, whilst at his work, Kerfoot came up to hi:a, knocked his lamp down, and threatened hint. Later on the same night Dickson also came up to him, knocked the lamp and broke two of its glasses, and struck the horse. Te damage done by Kerfoot was estimated at 2,1, and thee be- Dickson at Is G. 1.—10 defence it wee contended OW th complainant had made a mistake as to the defendants' iclen- titer, and witnesses were called in support of this contention. Ultimately the charges against Kerfoot were dismissed, eel Dickson was fined 13s 6,1, including damage, and costs ran: ehe first offence, and Os for the obstruction. DESPERATE STRUGGLE wrrn A. GARDEN THIEF.—AO elderly man named James Aspinall was charged at the ten Helens Police Court, on Mond ty' with having stolen some , cabbages and rhubarb from Miss Bishop's garden, Cowley Hill, on Sunday morning; and he was fur.her charged with t having assaulted P.C. Pope on the same occasion.—P.C. Pope said that at 5 o'clock on Sunday morning he was on ' duty on Cowley Hill in plain clothes, and saw the prisoner come out of Miss Elation's garden with cabbage and rhu- barb wader his arm. On seeing witness prisoner ran away, but was chased and overtaken in Cooper-street by witness. Aspinall attempted to get away by giving a false address, but on finding ebat this strategem did not sgcceed he re- sisted violently, threw witness down, kicked and struck him, and was not fairly secured till after a struggle of about 20 minutes' duration.-Supt. Johnston said pt ieoucr had been eight times previously convicted, and was con- victed of three separate offences of larceny on one day.— For the present larceny he was fined £2 and costs, or in de- fault one month's imprisonment; for the assault on the officer he was fined Ll and Costs, or in default a month's mprisonment. INCIPIENT BURGLARS AT Sr. HELENS. Three lads named Wirliam Shannon (8), Patrick Swift (9), and Chas. MnGhee (12), were charged at the St. Helens Police Court, on Wednesday, with having broken into the lock-up shop of John Edington, in Hardshaw-street, and stolen a quantity of articles therefrom.—A lad named James Braden 11 er!are of age, said that between 9 and 10 o'clock on Saturday night he met the three prisoners in Bold-street, and Shannon asked bim to go with them as they intended to break into a shop. He went with them to Mr. Edington's shop, and Shannon and Swift got over a wall into the backyard, whilst witness and McGhee stayed in thespassage. After Rome time Swift and Shannon returned over the wall, bringing a box of toffy and some corn plasters with them. Part of the toffy was shared amongst the four of them that night, and the rest on the Sunday afternoon. The box was broken up on the Sunday afternoon and burned. It appeared that the youths Shannon and Swift had obtained an entry to the shop by breaking a pane of glass in the back door and then undoing the fastenings. Besides the articles named some biscuits were also missed on the Monday morning, the total value stolen being 10s. On their apprehension the prisoners did not deny the charge, hnt began to accuse each °then—The Bench ordered Shannon and Swift to receive six strokes with a birch rod, and McGhee nine strokes. THE DANGER OF JUMPING ON FERRY BOATS : A Sr. HELENS CHILD DROWNED.—Mr. C. Aepinall, Liverpool borough coroner, held an inquest on Saturday afternoon on the body of Louisa Lea, 10 years of age, daughter of Joseph Lea, labourer, 63, Higher Parr-street, Bt. Helens, which was found floating in the river on Friday at the south end of the eight o'clock Saturday, in Lauding Stage. Witness, in reply to Mr. Palgrave Simpson, solicitor, who represented the Wallasey Local Board, said he was instructed to prevent people jumping on board. The jury, in returning a verdict of " Accidentel death," said they did not think anybody connected with the boat was to blame, but they suggested that there should be notices at the Wallasey berthea similar to those at the Birkenhead berths, cautioning, passengers from jumping on the boats when the gangways. are up.

He would limit the farms to 120 acres; but in order to meet the wants of the best class of labourers he would let the local authorities buy estates, make roads and and let out perpetual tenancies of trom zo to 30 acres, charging i per cent. over the rate at which the money had been bor- toWed. The holders under such a system would be virtual owners, subject to a ground rent, which would be collected with the rates, and at the end of 4.7 years the ground rent Would belong to the local authority. Such in brief is Mr. COLLINGS' scheme, it has:been received with considerable favour, and there i 8 no doubt that under such an arrangement !,he land would be made much more produc- itve ; for it is obvious that a person with a ,a.rhi of say from 5o to 100 acres is 41kely to put more energy and capital into ;the soil if he owns it than if he Si nply a tenant, with probably an inse- cure tenure and liable to have his rent in- ?rezil d on his own improvements or his skill lh farming. Something was said during the course of the debate on Friday to the effect that there was no monopoly in land, but that tatement is scarcely consistent with fact. -rrorn a return which was issued some years a.ge—and the salient points in which is given lo this year's Financial Refills Almanack—we 'tad that 72,119,961 acres of land in the nited Kingdom, producing a rental of 31,470,360, is held by 1,173,724. owners, 'which would seem to argue there is no 111„h1Iopoly ; but when an investigation of Luese owners is made it is found that only 2238 individuals hold altogether 39,924,232 4,CreS, which is 3,864,252 acres more than "alf the area ascribed to the 1,173,724 °lvners, and close upon sixteen millions of 4cpres more than a third part of the whole area °E Great Britain and Ireland. In this same turn—which was concocted to prove there ,W.as no land monopoly—these 2,238 indi- tVuals count as 3 804, for it is found "525 of ein hold land in two counties, 308 in three, 12,u6 in four, io6 in five, +I in six, 17 in seven, in eight, 9 in nine, 2 in ten, 3 in eleven, 2 41 twelve, and 2 in fourteen counties." aving regard to these facts it is absurd to t;_ay there is no monopoly, but if by any means IS Can be broken down and the land now 11, milled placed under cultivation, the better it will be for the country. It is not sur- trising that Mr. COLLINGS' scheme should aye aroused the ire of Mr. CHAPLIN. the ,‘tUernber for Mid-Lincoln, and other land- Tillers. Mr. CHAPLIN owns something like ti31'370 acres, his rent roll totals up to e respectable sum of £30,317, and any. 4gepreciatory observations of his must neces- u4,rilY be received with caution. He is one of who toil not neither do they spin, and V 45 attitude towards the Tenants Compensa- -I°n Bills is a convincing proof that he has Oftle in sympathy with the legitimate demands ti2ur agricultural population. His opposi, h" may, therefore, be dismissed as a purely tcletsonal and selfish one The moral to be 4.lrawn from the discussion on Mr. COLLINGS' 'tion is the desirability of as speedily as ssible en franchising the agricultural rPolation, and the necessity there exists them to be more directly re- vialiesented in order that their claims , be fairly treated. Until this is e coinplished there is little hope of their f:lancipation from their present unsatis- ct°rY condition.

THE BEASLEY BILL.—We understand that at the meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, on Wednesday next, Mr. R. bhaw will move a resolution to the effect that Dr. MacDougall, and those members of the Board who acted with him in the institution of the proceedings against Mr. Beasley, be requested to ref Lind to the Board the amount of costs already paid and to be paid by the Board in con- nection with the action Beasley v. Commissioners. The meeting will no doubt be a stormy one. WATEaLoo-BoAD SCHOOLS, WIDNES.—The managers of these schools have just received a donation of £25 from Messrs. Pilkingtons towards the cost of the proposed ex- tension.

Monmoms IN RUNCORN.—The disciples of Brigham Young have established a mission room in Cartwright-street, where services will be held once a month. Many years ago the Mormons had a branch of the faithful, which, how- ever, owing to removals and defections, had to be discon- tinued.

Sr. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.— The teachers and scholars attending this school had their annual treat on Monday, when they were conveyed to Overton Hills in four waggons. The Rev. E. Williams, the pastor, accompanied the excursionists, who spent a most enjoyable day on the hills. They were provided with tea and buns at Mersey View. RITNCORN PRISONER AT CHESTER ASSIZEL-At these Assizes this week, Edward Boden (33), a bricklayer, was charged with having, on the 15th inst., at Runcorn, entered the lock-up shop of Peter Sinnott, and stolen therefrom six shillings in money, a cheese, 2lbs. of bacon, and other articles. The prisoner was found guilty, and sentenced to nine months' imprisonment.

At the Liverpool county sessions, on Friday, Thomas Desmond (23), barber, and Letitia Desmoed (28' were in- dicted for stealing a gold watch, the property of Charles Etches, at Widnes, on the 25th April. Thomas Desmond was found guilty, and was sentenced to six months' im- prisonment with hard labour, and the female prisoner was acquitted.—Harriett Burns (26), no occupation, for wound- ing Emily Lightfoot, at Widnes, on the 2nd inst., was sen- tenced to six months' imprisonment with hard labour. ST. EDWARD'S ROMAN CATHOLIC SCHOOLS, RUNCORN.— The scholars attending the day and Sunday schools in con- nection with St. Edward's Roman Catholic Church had their annual treat on Tuesday, when, accompanied by the Rev. Father Ferment; and the teachers they were conveyed by the noon train to irrodsham, where they spent a pleasant day. The children were supplied with a substantial tea, and the teachers offered them prizes for competition in various games. ST. Ewes CHURCH, WIDNES.—The building committee of this church have, after much much consideration, decided to let the contract for the chancel, and the work will be car- ried out by Messrs. Morrison and Son, Wavertree. It is estimated that this will save the sum of £5OO, as an extra wall would have had to be built if the transepts only were proceeded with as at first intended. The tower and boun- dary wall will be erected at some future period when furiber funds are forthcoming. THE ROBBERY AT SINNOTT'S SHOP, RUNCORN.—At Chester Assizes, on Monday, in the Case of breaking into Peter Sinnott's shop, Waterloo-road, Runcorn, and stealing a large quantity of articles, the Grand Jury found "no bill "against Cartwright. On the same evening the accused arrived in Runcorn by train, and was met at t'ee railway station by several hundreds of men, women, and children, who made a demonstratie n in his favour. On Tuesday B Alen was found guilty of the robbery, and was sentenced te nine months' hard labour. LOCAL ExIIIBITORS AT SOUTHPORT AGRICULTURAL SHOW.—Amongst the local exhibitors at the 27th annual show of the Ormskirk, Southport, and Bootle A ericialtural Society, held at Southport, on Wednesday, the following carried off prizes for dogs :—Non-sporting division.—Mas- tiff, dog or bitch: 1, H. C. Joplin, Ruyton. St. Bernard, dog or bitch: 1 and 2, H. C. Joplin; 3, W. M. Pothecary, Lymm. Collie dog or bitch (smooth coded): 1, H. C. Joplin. Bull terrier, dog or bitch: 3, H C. Joplin.—Spert- ing division.—Pointer, dog or bitch: 3, J. Mathieson, War- rington. Greyhound, bitch: 1, H. C. Joplin; 2, G. H. Yates, Farnworth.—Mr. W. Whitlow, of Preston Brook, was one of the judges of heavy horses. MELANCHOLY FATALITY AT HOUGH GREEN.—A sad ac- cident happened at Hough Green, on Wednesday night, to Miss Elizabeth Houghton, who kept a small draper's shop there. Miss Houghton, who was between 50 and 60 years of age, was in the house alone, when she upset a paraffin lamp, and spilt some of the burning oil upon her clothing, which was qta7ckly in a blaze. Her screams attracted the attention of the neighbours, who came to her assistance and extinguished the flames. Dr. Booth, of Farnworth, was sent for, and found that the unfortunate woman was severely burnt about the legs and the lower part of the body. She lingered in great agony until Thursday morning, when she expired. The deceased was formerly in the employ of Lady Stapleton, at Ditton Hall. CRUELTY TO A. HORSE.—A greengrocer named James Taylor, of Albert-road, Widnee, was summoned at Warring- ton Police Court, on Monday, for having ill-used a horse by working it while in an unfit condition.—Enspector Lewis, of the R.S.P.C.A., said that on the 4th inst. he, in company with Inspect& Singleton, found defendant in Warrington in charge of a grey mare which was suffering from a sup- purated wound on the back. The wound was about the size of a two-shilling piece, and the horse was in great pain. At his request the animal was taken out of the shafts of the cart to which it was attached.—lnspector Singleton cor- roborated.—Defendant contended that the wound had been caused after he left Widnes on the day in question. and be produced a certificate from Mr. Haynes to the effect that the horse was fit for work.—The Bench considered the case proved, and fined defendant 2s 6d and 13s costs. PROMENADE CONCERTS AT RUNCORN.—Tbe Mill Brow Sunday School Brass Bard, under the conductorship of Mr. J. Ainsworth, played the following programme on the Mereet-place, on Thursday evening :—March, " Univer- sity " ; anthem, "Jerusalem, my glorious home"; chorus, "Vital spark " ; anthem, "Let every heart rejoice " ; althem, "Pheenix Park"; anthem, •'Hark, the song of jueilee "; "God save the Queen." These open air concerts have been a great success, the various performances having drawn vast crowds of orderly listeners, and to Mr. Dutton great credit is due for the labour he undertook in inaugurat- ing them. There has been considerable expense attending the concerts in providing forms, stands, music, itc., and although Mr. Dutton's appeal for subscriptions has been pretty generously responded to, he is still a good sum out or pocket. It is to be hoped that Mr. Dutton will not suffer f it- the disinterested part he has taken, and that those who have received enjoyment and benefit from the excellent music discoursed by the bands will contribute their mite towards the expenses. Feeran RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR WIDNES.—On Tues- day evening, at the Cock and Trumpet Inn, Halebank-road, Mr. T. W. Barker, the coroner, hold an inquiry touching the death of John Fendick, who was injured on the rail- way on the 17th inst. Mr. Ferrand, from the solicitors' department, Lime-street Station, represented the London and North-Western Railway Companyeand Mr. Roberts, engineer for the contractor, appeared on behalf of Mr. Evans. It appeared from the evidence given by Thos. Turner, engine- driver, and Mary Cox, sister of the deceased, that the de- ceased was employed as a shunter to the workmen of Mr. James Evans, contractor for the Widnes and Speke exten- sion of the London and North-Western Railway Company. About seven o'clock on the 17th inst. the deceased was en- gaged at his occupation, and uncoupled a waggon from a number of others. As he was stepping from between then the buffer caught his thigh, which received a severe wrench, and he was taken home by a fellow-workman named Brown. The serious nature of his injuries did not appear to have been at first realised, and Fendick rapid,y grew worse, and died on Saturday morning. Dr. O'Keeffe attended him up to his decease.—A verdict of "Accidental death" Wan re- turned. ROBBERY WITH VIOLENCE AT RUNCORN.—At the Chester Assizes, on Wednesday, Henry Brindrick (28), labourer, and Catherine Bowden, a woman described as having no occupation, were charged with having, at Runcorn, on the 28th of April, robbed Frederick Hancock, with violence, of a watch guard. Mr. J. E. Bankes was for the prosecution, and Mr. Douglas for the defence.—lt appeared that about 11 o'clock on the 28th of April prosecutor wos going with a friend named Foster to his residence in Blantvre-street, and when he was passing under an arch near his house the female prisoner seized him by the arm, and the male prisoner struck him a violent blow, by which he was knocked down. When he was on the ground Brindrick kicked him and robbed him of his watch guard. Mr. Foster went to the prosecutor's assistance, but he was knocked down by a male accomplice of the prisoners. The two men and the woman then ran away. Two days afterwards she took the watch guard to a pawnshop, and, it being suspected that the art;cle had been stolen, she was detained and taken into custody. She then confessed her guilt, and incriminated the male pri- soner. When he was arrested she accused him of having suggested the robbery and taken part in it, and he acknow- ledged that he was guilty.—The prisoners were found guilty. There being a previous conviction for a similar offence against each of the prisoners. Brindrick was sentenced to penal servitude for ten years, end the female prisoner to penal servitude for five years.

PRECAUTIONS AgAINST CHOCRRA.

The DEPUTY CLERK read an order from the Local Govern- ment Board, and a report from Captain Clark, of Weston, with regard to cholera. The latter suggested that the cut near "No man's land" should be the anchorage for vessels arriving with sickness on board, but said from his experi- ence the disease was more likely to be imported in small coasters than in foreign vessels.—A committee, consisting of the Chairman, the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, Mr. John Ashton, and Mr. E. A. Wallington was appointed to deal with the matter.

PAUPERISM IN LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRR.-We have extracted the following from a Local Government return relating to the state of pauperism at Midsummer and Chris- mas last :-Lancashire: In this county, with a population of 3,485,611, there were 21,543 indoor paupers at Midsum- mer. Of these 1,818 were able-bodied adults and 1,738 children, against 24,060. Of these 2,731 were able-bodied adults and 2,143 children. At Christmis 5,419 males, 5,218 females, and 4,209 children were not able-bodied, against 8,452 males, 5,494 females, and 4,206 children. 1,136 males, 1,378 females, and 92 children were lunatics or idiots, against 1,144 males, 1 385 females, and 151 children. There were 535 vagrants in the several unions, against 454. There were 48,003 outdoor paupers, against 51,105 Of these 1,200 were adult males, 6,500 females, and 18.764 were children able-bodied, against 1,675 males, 7.066 females, and 20,248 children. There were 3,790 ,males, 11,133 females, and 2.216 children not able-bodied, against 3,935 males, 11,452 females, and 2,317 children. There were 1,932 males, 2,365 females, and 48 children idiots or lunatics, against 2,073 males, 2,254 females, and 34 children.-Ckeshire : In this county there were 3.090 indoor paupers, against 3,262. Of the former 188 males, 342 females, and 321 children were able-bodied, against 282 males, 339 females, and 353 children. There were 667 males, 372 females, and 768 children not able-bodied, against 781 males, 361 females, and 756 children. The lunatics and idiots numbered 113 males, and 169 females. and 8 children, against 110 males, 155 females, and 11 children. There were 10,736 outdoor paupers against 10,714. Of the former 133 males. 1,148 females, and 3,399 children were able-bodied, against 154 males, 1,173 females, and 3 391 children. The not able-bodied numbered 1,199 males, 3,162 females, and 652 children. against 1,183 males, 3,188 females, and 642 children. There were 463 males, 566 females, and 8 children lunatics or idiots, against 440 males, 651 females, and 8 children,

div.head: ANTROBUS WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: THE ANTROBUS WATER SUPPLY.

The DEPUTY CLERK read the evidence he had obtained with regard to Barber's well at Antrotins, from which it ap- peared that the well was a public one. He advised that counsel's opinion be taken on the matter and as to the steps the Authority should take to assert their right to the well. —On the motion of Mr. E. A. WALLINUFON scotiled uy Mr. JOHN ASISCON, it was decided to adopt the course sug- gested.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO A WIDNES
div.p: PRESENTATION TO A WIDNES
CURATE.

As we announced a short time ago, the Rev. W. H. Duggan is about to vacate the curacy of Widnes Parish Church, and take up his residence in Manchester, and on Friday evening last week. the Sunday school teachers and a good number of parishioners, met in Waterloo-road schools for the purpose of wishing him "God speed" in his new , sphere of labour, and to present him with a token of their regard. The Rev. J. WRIGHT WILLIAMS the vicar, presided, and in the name of the Sunday school teachers and scholars asked Mr. Duggan to accept a handsome marble timepiece, which bore the following inscription "Presented to the Rev. W. H. Duggan, by the Parish Church Sunday schools, Widnes, July 20th 1883. "—Mr. CRABTREn said it afforded him great pleasure to take part in promoting the presen- tation, and he was sure Mr. Deggan had the hearty good wishes of all in Simm's Cross school, for his future success and happiness.—Mr. litEcaoss remarked th tt the youngest children in Waterloo-road scnools, had added their mite to the cost of the gift.—The Rev. W. H. DUGGAN accepted the valuable present with feelings of pleasure and gratitn le. The gift was a suitable one, for as he marked the flight of time he should think of an approaching re-union in a better land, and remember that it was necessary to be diligent and faithful in saving souls, for "the night cometh when no man can work." He had spent many happy hours amongst them, and he should always be glad to hear of their welfare and the success of their schools. (Applause )—Mr. J. B. 'miaow then read the following address:—" To the Rev. W. He Duggan.—Dear Sir,—The parishioners of Widnes desire, on your resignation of this curacy, to offer you some mark of their recognition of your untiriree and energetic labours during the time (now nearly three years) you have been among them. Will you, therefore, accept this address and accompanying purse of gold, as a small token of the respect in which you are held by them. Heartily wishing you every success in your new sphere of labour, and pray- ing for God's blessing on your work, we are, dear Mr. Duggan, on behalf of the parishioners, yours very truly, JOHN B. IMISON, LEWIS KILOROSS, cttirchsvard,ns —Widnes, July 20th, 1883."—Mr. Curran, Mr Farrant, and Mr. Frank Cave spoke a few words appropriate to the occasion, and the Chairman thco presented the address and the purse of gold.—ln response, the Rev. W. H. DUGGAN expressed his obligations to the church- wardens and the collectors, especially the ladies uho had acted both courageously and kindly. He thanked the sub- scribers, for he knew that the money came out of the pockets of those who c( uld not spare much, and therefore represented more than money usually did. He must acknowledge the courtesy and kindness of nearly all with whom he had come in contact. He bad met many friends in the truest and fullest sense of the word, and he would always befriend them if be could. He felt these tokens of esteem more than be could express, and concluded by acknowledging the present that the chairman had himself made him, which would be of great benefit to him in his future life. (Appleuse.)—A vote of thanks to the Vicar for presiding brought the pro- ' ceedings to a close.

div.head: SMART CAPTURE OF A RUNCORN
div.p: SMART CAPTURE OF A RUNCORN
ROBBER.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. H. Reynolds and Mr. John Brundrit, Ernest Baughen, 17 years of age, was; brought up in custody charged with stealing £.4, and a coa,, .Aild vest of the value of .£1 103, the monies ai goods of Aaron log.gett. The prosecutor said he re- sided at stoke, County ILI ch,.-.7 wall, and was the mister of the vessel called did "Lancashire .Sturd On ynight, about half-past 10, -1(, put his purse, cote.2,ning 411Ps in in gold and some silver, under the pillow of his ,in fr!' cabin on board the vessel On Sand ty evening he examined it and found that .t 1 in gold had been abstracted. Next morning at six o'clock he missed the prisoner, who was an apprentice with him, and subsequently discovered that a coat and vest which had been worn by another apprentice had been taken away. The cost and vest produced were his property. The vessel was lying in the tidal dock at Runcorn.—lnspector Hollingworth stated that from information he received from the last witness, on Monday morning he telegraphed to the authorities at Scotland Yard the name and description of the prisoner, who was arrested in London the same evening wearing the stolen apparel and with over £3 in his pocket. On his arrival at Runcorn on the previous day, the prisoner admitted that he had stolen four sovereigns.—P.C. Kelly deposed to receiving the prisoner in custody from the metropolitan police at Willesden.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The Rev. Canon Barclay presided over the meeting held at the Workhouse, Dutton, on Tuesday. Present—The Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, Messrs. J. Ashton, W. Handley, J. Higbfield, J. Stokes, T. Norman, J. Mclntyre, J. Smith, C. Rigby, J. Midsvood, W. Jackson, J. Darbyshire, J. Weir, E. A. Wallington, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). TRH BOARD AND THE LIVERPOOL INFIRMARY.

In accordance with the notice which he had given, Mr. HANDLEY proposed that the Board contribute an annual subscription of £5 to the Liverpool Infirmary. He pointed out that the Board paid a subscription of £3 to the Manchester Infirmary, and the Board sent sometimes two and three ca.,. a year. Liverpool was easier of access to the greater portion of the residents in the Board's district, and it would be a great convenience if the Board could send those who could not afford to go themselves. • Mr. NORMAN endorsed Mr. fluidity's observations, and could not see why they should not subscribe to Liverpool as well as Manchester. He seconded the motion. Mr. WEIR proposed an amendment that the Board pay three guineas a year, whether it wal to Manchester or Liver- pool. He thought they ought to be more careful of the ratepayers' money and not :Tend it in the lavish manner suggested. Mr. WALLINGTON: But if you withdraw the subscription- from Manchester you can aff .rd to give £5 to Liverpool. Rev. J. Locawoon seconded the amendment. Mr. C. EWE,/ considered it was perfectly ridiculous to spend in this way money that people had had to work hard for. The amendment was carried by a large majority, only mover and seconder of the original motion voting for it.

VISITING COMMITTEE. Mr. HANDLEY presented the report of the Visiting Com- mittee, who advised the Board that the suggestions of Mr. Dansey, with regard to the house, should be carried out as they thought, the sanitary condition of the house would be improved. As to the adoption of toe Casual Poor Act, the committee had deferred that question until next meeting Si) that Mr. Jcnes could furnish them with certain int,rmation they ruquired. Mr. Jones informed the committee that he had occasionally found it necessary to detain vagrants longer than usual; under the Casual Poor Act, and the committee wished to know what the effect of that unusual detention had been.—Mr. HANDLEY moved and Mr. PARBYSHIRE ; seconded the adoption of the report, which motion was ' carried. STATE or THE HOUSE. The M.ister (Mr. Jones) reported that there were 177 in- mates in the house against 169 in the corresoonding week last year. 39 boys and 29 girls were at school, and two boys and 10 girls were receiving imins,rial training. Outdoor relief had been administered to 653 persons at a total cost of £67 16s. 3d, against 614 persons in the corresponding week last year, at a cost of £65 7s. 11d,

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
At Cornwall Assizes, yesterday, Joha Mayne pleaded guilty to extensive hands on the Dolcoath Mine, and was sentenced by Lord Coleridge to seven years' penal ser- vitude.

A supplementary estimate was issued yesterday morning for £300,790. Of this sum £200;0049 is required for addi- tional expenses in connection with the introduction of six- penny telegrams; £45,000 for the purchase of the Ashburn- ham Manuscripts ; and £1,500 for rewards to persons through whom dynamiters were convicted. On Thursday night, between eight and nine o'clock, Edward Swain, a boatman employed at Stubb's pleasure boat establishment on the river Dee, was fastening the boats up for the night, when he overbalanced himself and fell into deep water and was drowned, before a rescue could be effJeted.

On Thursday evening an old man named George Ger- rard, who lives by himself in Market-street, Crewe, made a determined attempt on his life. Some neighbours hearing groans from his dwelling, went in and found him with his throat cut in several places. A sharp knife and steel covered with blood were found on the table close by. Medical aid was obtained, but yesterday morning Gerrard was in a very precarious condition.

div.head: ACCIDENT 10 THE DUKE OF CAMBRIDGE.
div.p: ACCIDENT 10 THE DUKE OF CAMBRIDGE.

The Duke of Cambridge had just alighted from a carriage at Chatham, on Thursday night, when the horses suddenly turned, and the carriage struck him in the chest. He was only slightly hurt. MURDER OF A SOLDIER.

Yesterday morning, between twelve and one o'clnck, Cor- poral Ernest Hope, of the Ist Battalion of the East Kent Regiment, was shot dead by Private Wilson of the same regiment. Wilson and Hope lived in the same room in Linen Hall Barracks, and on the latter coming off sentry duty he deliberately shot the other dead while he was lying in his bed. Wilson was at once arrested and said that he did not know why he committed the deed as he and the de- cased were always great friends. THE BOLTON OUTRAGE: ANOTHER DEATH.

Yesterday morning, Patrick Kelly, who was assaulted with a clever by ht s brother a week ago, in Antelope-court, Bolton, died at the ir.firmary from his injuries. From the first his recovery had been hopeless, his skull being frac- tured and his brain laid bare. This is the second death, the perpetrator of the outrage, Peter Kelly, dying from concus- sion of the brain, sustained by jumping from a bedroom win- dow. Mrs. Kelly, who was also attacked, will recover.
MR. BRAIkAUGH'S ACTION AGAINST THE SERGEANT-AT-ARMS.

We are informed that the Solicitors to the Treasury entered an appearance, on Thursday, for the Sergeant-at- Arms to the action brought by Mr. Bradlaugh, and that Messrs. Lewis at once delivered the statement of claim. The case will probably be heard on motion next Thursday. Mr. Bradlaugh will argue in person befcre the Divisional Court, and the Attorney-General will, pursuant to the order of the House of Commons, appear for the Sergeant- at-Arms.
SERIOUS COLLISION IN THE CHANNEL A SHIP SUNK AND THREE LIVES LOST.

A special cable message just received from Malta, dated 6 p.m. Thursday, states that the steamer Glenogle, from London via Suez, to Singapore, Hong Kong, and hangbai, has put into the harbour at Valetta, and reports that soon after leaving the Thames, when near the Sovereign Shoal Liethtship, she came into collision with the barque Achilles, 556 tons register, which almost immediately sank, three of the crew going down with the slain. The remainder were rescued, and have been carried on to Malta and landed there. The Achilles at the time of the disaster was bound from Buenos Ayres to Antwerp with a full cargo of wool, hides, &c., valued at £15,000. TERRIBLE GUN TRA.GEDY.

A gun accident had a sad end with a young gentleman and his Littler, on nursday night. While David Arnott, son of Mr. Arnett, warehouseman, Glasgow, and nephew of Sir John Arnott, of Dublin, was engaged working with a small pistol in a room in his father's coast house at Blair. more, Argyleshire, he placed the weapon to the side of his head, and, being unaware that it was loaded, drew the trigger, when the contents entered his head close to the ear. fie ituntadiately became insensible. The unfortunate young man was about seventeen years of age, and died the sane night. Ilia father died shortly after hearing of the occurrence. THE WFSLEYAN CONFERENCE.

The \Vesleyan Conference met in Hull yesterday morn- ing at half-past nine o'clock, and took up the question of candidates for the ministry. In the course of a conversa- tion, it was stated that there were 99 who are without cir- cuits, also eight missionaries for whom circuits must be found. The C.mference then proceeded to examine the qualifications of the 53 candidates recommended by their resptctive district committees, when 38 were accepted. The ex-president announced a gift of £5O from the proprietors of the new Wesleyan paper Joyful News to the Auxiliary Fund. The division of circuits, additional ministers, and district missionaries were not considered. A proposal to appoint the Rev. Hugh Price Hughes as connexional evan- gelist, led to a discussion, when it was decided to grant him the assistance of a junior minister for the ensuing year. Several official appointments were made, and the Conference adjourned. THE CONDITION OF ARMENIA.

Addressing a meeting at Steinway Hall, London, yester- day afternoon, convened by the Committee of Turkish Missions Aid Society, to consider the present condition of Armenia and Armenians, Earl Carnarvon said every states- min who had been cilled to deal with the Armeni in ques- tion had pointcd to the great danger to the peace of Europe if the existing state of affairs were allowed to continue. All that the Armenians demanded was self-government under a proper governor, and they certainly did not amount to a demand for absolute independence. If this concession were grant€d he believed contentment wonld take the place of dis,ffection, and the strongest barrier would be erected against Russian intrigue and aggression. THE CHOLERA.

The following telegrams have been received at the War Office from the Goner Al Officer commanding in Egypt : " Cairo, 26th July. Died of cholera on the 22nd, Piivate J. Mundle, Black Wiitch. Oa 23rd, Private E. Shoesmith, Black Watch. On 24th, Privates Michael Corrigan, J. Smith, T. Dodds, and J. Cameron, Highlanders; also Pri- vates J. Fraser and H. Matthews, Black Watch ; also Cor- poral W. Stevens and Private I'. Smith, Army Hospital Corps; also Lieutenant Lrquesne, Royal Artillery. On 25th, Corporal Cooper and Private Anderson, King's Rifles; also Corporal Gardner, 2nd Brigade, E.A. On 26th, Private McKey and Private Phillips, Black Watch." (A note appended to foregoing telegram says, regimental numbers of three of the men have been telegraphed for, there being more than one of same name in regiment.) "Cairo, 27th July. Health of Cornwall Regiment improv- ing. Total tohniasions for cholera, 2 officers and 34 men ; deaths, 2 officers and 23 men. Deaths stnce yesterday's telegram, Lieutenant Croft, R.A., and eight men, whose names and numbers will be given.

WARRINGTON WATERWORKS.

From the report of the proceedings at the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, on Tuesday, it will be seen that the attention of the Chamber was directed to the water supply of the borough, and to the necessity there exists for greater provision being made against an outbreak of fire. The supply, we believe, is ample, but the pressure —in the event of a conflagration of any mag- nitude—is insufficient. As a result of the discussion it was resolved "That a memorial from the Chamber be presented to the Corporation respectfully asking them to consider the desirability of purchasing the waterworks in the general interest of the ratepayers." It is almost un- necessary for us to say that the Corporation have had this matter under consideration more than once, and though there can scarcely be two opinions about the advantages which would accrue from the works being under the control of the Council, still, from a variety of reasons they have not as yet been able to accomplish this. Once indeed, somewhere about twenty or twenty-three years ago, the Corporation proposed to go to Parliament for powers to purchase compulsorily, but the ratepayers stepped in and prevented this being done. It was at that time thought alike by the Corporation and the Company that there would be little difficulty about the matter, and that the purchase, if completed, would not be an adverse one to the Corporation. Again, in 1878, when the Company were promoting a bill in Parliament for additional powers, a, proposal was made to them for the purchase of the under- taking by the Corporation, the basis suggested being that adopted in buying the gasworks welch was one of 19 years' purchase on a year's profit. The committee who then acted on behalf of the Corporation comprised Messrs. John Fairclough (Mayor), John Burgess, S. M. Webster, Edward Milner, C. J. Holmes, and Josh. Davies, and their report (which is dated 7th January, 1878") contain- ing the terms agreed upon tiy them concludes as follows :—" We have drawn up .this report SO as to satisfy the request of the directors of the War, ington Waterworks Company that some counter offer should he made, and in reply to the letter of their chairman asking for the views of the Council on the Bill." This would seem 'to indicate the Company wanted to sell, but be that as it may, the negotiations at that time did not come to anything, the company in view, we believe, of the powers they were seeking not considering the occasion opportune to effect a transfer. Since then Lints have from time to time been dropped in the Council Chamber as to the desirability of ac- quiring the works, and, if we mistake not, towards the close of the last municipal year a committee of the Corporation sounded the Company on the point, with what result has not transpired. We have no doubt that now active steps will be taken—as they certainly ought to be—with the ob- ject of getting the undertaking transferred to the Corpora- tion, and in view of that it may be worth while to place before our readers a statement of the wital of fi..e company as in 1878—when a committee of the Corporation last formally dealt with the subject—and as it now stands in the balance sheet made up to the end of last year. In the report of the committee of the Corporation. , already alluded to, the capital stands as follows :-3,000 shares at £lO paid, dividend limited to 10 per cent, £30,000; 1,500 shares at £lO paid, dividend limited to 71 per cent., £15,000; and 3.000 sharesat £lO paid, dividend limited Ito 7 per cent., £3o,ooo—together £75,000; to which add loans on mortgage, estimated at £20,000—£95.000; and further expenditure on capital account, estimand at £3,000, giving a total of £98,000. The committee add:—"lt would appear from the company applying for further Par- liamentary powers that a considerable increase of expendi- ture on capital account is contemplated, and it is a matter for serious consideration as to whether the manufactuting requirements of the borough will increase so as to meet the revenne that this outlay requires." The committee gave the total cost of the works at that time as "nearly £100,000." From the balance sheet made up to the 30th December last we find the cesteof the works to 30th June 1812 wal £138,879 5s 63, in addition to which there has been spent on town extensions £69 4s, and on the new works at Winwick £2,299 15s 104, making a total ex- pendituure on the works of £141,248 5s 4d.. towards which the Company have raised £140,99S 2s 10,1, or £250 2s 6tl short of the amount expended. THE ROME SECTARY AND THE BLASPHEMY PROSECUTIONS. Si-7,-10a Tuesday evening, in the House of Commons, it W. Harcourt made a statement to the eNect that he had Teceived a number of memorials praying for the release of Messrs Foote and Ramsey, now imprisoned in Holloway -Gaol for blasphemy. He also stated that those gentlemen who had signed the memorial could not have seen the libels ityquestion, which, he'said, were to his mind obscene, and a 'scandalous outrage on public decency. Now, I have had an opportunity to thoroughly peruse the Christmas number of the Freethinker, in which the eatd libels were. I cannot mate out how ffir W. 'Harcourt can say there was anything indecent in it. Lord Chief Justine Coleridge was of the opinion that the charge could not be maintained. There are plenty of books published that contain far more blas- phemy than the Freethinker. I have a book out of the War- rington Library at the present time, entitled "The Earth- ward Pilgrimage," by M. D. Conway, which is one of this class of books. No one ever dreams of prosecuting the author or publishers of this book, yet the blasphemy con- tained in it is as much a crime as that in the Freethinker. -Freedom of thought and of epeech is one of the first prin- ciples of Liberalism; and is it not a shame that in this nineteenth century, and in a country like England—boast- ing as it does of being the freest country in the world—two men should be imprisoned for twelve and nine months respectively for simply hurting people's feelings? Christians can scarcely expect Freethinkers to respect their feelings when they are so ready to slander and villify any atheist they come across. But the question is, ought a Secretary of State to allow his private epiniqns to guide him in a matter so serious as this? He received a memo- rial the other week, signed by some of the leading scientific and professional men of the day. Does he suppose these men would attach their signatures to a memorial of this sort without being acquainted with the conditions under which the imprisonment of Messrs. Foote and Ramsay was brought about? Four thousand people assembled in St. James's Hall, London, to remonstrate against this great wrong, but the Home Secretary has taken no notice of this. I beg the insertion of this in your next issue that it may call the attention of all true Liberals to this most un- warrantable and illiberal act of the Home Secretary.—l am, A YOUNG REFORMER. Warrington, July, 1883.

The Romish Davies summoned Margaret Hughes for using defamatory Church asserts that the Reformation robbed it of language to her. The case was dismlysed all that the Protestant Church now calls her own. This, I have no doubt, is so; but the people found themselves seated betwixt two stools, and of course came to the ground. Dissent sprung up as soon as the faggot was quenched, but it has I always found a bitter enemy in the Church, which taught that no tyranny on the part of a sovereign could justify re- k hellion. The ground, therefore, taken now, is that the wealth of the Cburch was given for the benefit et the nation, and must revert to the nation—that is the people. The wealth of the Church of England is enormous. Two- thirds of the produce of the land is subject to tithes, and as the annual produce of the land was calculated many years ago at £132,500,000, this would give £8,800,000. But this has increased immensely. One-third of the titheable property in the kingdom has come into existence during the last century. The Archbishop of Canterbury in 1848 re- turned his income at £3,951, but the rent of his leased estates was £16,236, or £12,825 more than he returned his income at. I give this as an instance of the easy con- science the clergy are proverbially possessed of. One of the main arguments relied upon by Dissenters in their endeavours to disestablish the Church, is that the parsons look too much after the loaves and fishes, and neglect their flock. This has now become proverbial. Scarcely a day passes without the Times containing a lealer setting forth the gross absurdity of allowing a class of men—generally speaking ignorant men—to set themselves up as teachers of the people. Lord Bramwell, speaking on the Deceased Wife Sister's Bill, said the teachings of the "theologians had been the cause of mere unhappiness and sins in the world than any- thing else." It is evident from this that all we have to say to the parsons may be summed up in a few words:—" You have had a grand opportunity for doing good, you have had immense sums of money at your disposal; where shall we find the good you have done with it? We are told that England to-day is to a great extent in a more benighted state than some of the lands to which missionaries are sent, and still you want this state of things to continue. Your property is national property, it is yours merely in trust; and the nation may at any time resteme possession of it. Do not contend that the nation has no such right. If the nation through its Parliament has now no right to meddle with Church property, it never could have had such a right at any time in history; therefore, the seizure and transfer of property of the Catholic Church under Henry VIII was an actof violence and tyranny, and you should be made to dis- gorge." The Duke of Bedford owns property worth more £50,000 a year, and the Duke of Norfolk Januwl Property worth over £lOO,OOO a year, all derived from the Catholic Church through the loving kindnese-of bluff King Hal. Of the 13,261 benefices in the Church, the members of the House of Lords have the right of presentation to 4,521. What, too, can we think of a Church which allows that divine gentleman' the Prince of Wales, the Paragon of pigeon shooters, to hold sa the patronage of 76 livings. To y that all this money belongs to the Church is fals% No matter how the Church acquired it; no matter who left it to the clergy; it must be taken back again and given to the people. Nay, more than this, thievery buildings must be turned to useful work. Look•any Sunday inside Trinity Church, and yeti find a ,mere handful of people, the officers of the church outnumbering the congregation. Let this church be turned into a lecture hall, the living diverted froin the wasteful channel through which it now flows, into paying able and learned lecturers, and we should soon see an alteration in the grim looking pile. Sir, I have no doubt that there are good easy souls who will say that Ibis is outrageous talk. Such people know little of what is daily done in our midst by the clergy. Pluralism of the most unblushing character is rampant. I could almost fill your paperaeith cases of such, for the present I give one or two. Canon Rowsell gets a still at Westminster' has a valuable West End living, and is deputy-clerk of the closet to the Queen whatever that may mean. The late Senior Canon of Gloucester, the Rev. , Sir John H. Culme Seymour, Bart., had in addition to his canonry the rectory of Northchurch, which is in the gift of the Prince of Wales, and is valued at £9lO a year and a house, with a population of 1,886. He was appointed Chap- lain in Ordinary to the Queen in 1827, Prebendary of Leicester St. Margaret in Lincoln Cathedral with an income of £72 attached, Canon Resident of filoupeoger Cathedral in 1829 with an income

Blinkhoin and Alderman Maryde UNLICENSED HAWKING—Mary Gallagher was fineJ 24 6d and costs for hawking antamacassars, Ac., IR Kirkland-street, on the Wednesday previous without a license. REFUSING TO QUIT.—WiI tarn Hirst was fined 1O ad coes for having refused to quit the Sefton Arms on eaturday afternoon.—Defenclant, it appeared, had refused to leave when requested t 3 do so by the landlady, and had to be ejected by a policeman. BREAmfirs OF THE PEACE.—WWinM Mulligan was bound over for one month for having co:nmitted a breach of the peace on Saturday last.

PRESCOT PETTY SESSIONS. TVESDAY.—Before Messrs. Whits and blinkhorn. RESISTING THE POLICE.—Mary Cartier Pre.c3t, wns fined 108 and costs for attempting to re.cue a pawner from the custody of P.O. Ormerod on the 30th ult.
The American rifle team paid a visit to Windsor yester- day, and were conducted over the Castle.

John Swift and James O'Leary, two men connected with a gang of female personators in Liverpool, were on Tues- day committed for trial by Mr. Mansfield, charged with being concerned in the theft of a gold watch and chain. Two other accused persons, Thomas and Ellen Cale, were also committed for trial for robbing Thomas Higginson. Mr. Justice Field bad before him at Chester Assizes on Thursday an action in which the Rev. G. A Butterton. of Eby], sued his solicitor, Mr. W. R. Williams, for £5,000 damages, consequent on unremunerative property dealings in which the plaintiff, ir,y Mr. Williams's advice, bad em- barked. Following - a consultation, however, counsel intimated that a satisfactory arrangement had been made, whereby all imputations were withdrawn, and the defendant undertook all liability in connection with the properties originating the dispute. His Lordship commended the mutual willingness to avoid an embittering contest which had been displayed.

THE STRIKE IN THE IRON TRADE.—The ironmasters of South Staffordshire, at a meeting iu Birmingham, on Thurs- day, resolved that, unless the itonworkers yet on strike complied with the award for a reduction of wages, ani resumed work, a general lock-out should be established throughout the district. A contemplation of the poverty and misery which would be entailed upon a community of some forty thousand operatives by their cutnpulsory idleness and consequent loss of wages will, it is hoped, prevent the small minority who still remain on strike in the West Brow wich and Oldbury districts from holding out. Many thousands of the men have already resumed work ; the strike has been condemned and is discountenanced by the leading trade association as a fogrant breach of contract; and it i- hopid that calmer counsels will prevail to rescue the dis- trict from the hardships which an enforced stoppage of al. its productive industries would bring about. The 13 operatives who are cliarA,;k-d oith riotous assembly and damaging works were on Thursday c,Annaitted to the assizes for trial.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. BATURDAY.—There was no business for disposal. MONDAY.—Before Alderman PiCkMere, Major Cartwright, and Mr. John rairclough. BEGGING —John Wainwright, an old man, and Robert Kip- pie, a young man, were each sent to gaol for 14 days for begging. PITCH AND Toss.—flenry Smith, George Allen, Joseph Cox, Henry Riley, and Jonah Palmer, respectable looking youths, were summoned for playing at pitch and toss on a footpath tetween Bewsey Bridge and Froghall-lane. on Sunday, the 15th inst.—Defendants, with the exception of Riley, pleaded guilty, and were ordered to pay 3s 6d each, the summons against Riley being dismissed. THROWING STONES.— Two boys, named William Parnell and Richard Holmes, both living in the neighbourhood of Warbur- ton-s'reet, were ordered to pay 3s 6d each for throwing stones on the highway. \ ODSTRITCTING TICE FOOTPATH.—James Appleton. Bank- street, was fined 2s 6d for obstructing the footpath in Bank- street by wheeling a coal wagon thereon. TUESDA.Y.—Betore Major Cartwright and Councillor Monks. The only case of interest will be sound reported in another column. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Davies and Alderman ()handley. The businesl will be found reported in another column. THIIRSDAY.—Before Captain Litton and Alderman Webster. The business will be found reported in another column. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds and Mr. John White Tin MAINTENANCE OF A MOTHER.—George Allen, black- smith, 35, Maryland street, Stratford New Town, Essex, was summoned, but did not appear. to show eau e why he should not contribute towards the maintenance of his mother, Pnoebe Allen, who has become chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union —Mr. J. C. Sutton, clerk to the Guardians, said that the woman lived with one of her sons in Warrington. That son had kept her, and was willing to help her when he was in a position•to do so, but some weeks back he fell ill, and the woman was now receiving 3s per week outdoor relief. The .defendant had written several letters to the Guardians in reply to letters from them, saying that he was unable to pay Is 6d per week, the amount asked for by the Guardians. He ad- mitted that he was receiving 36s per week, but said he had a wife and six children to keep, and bad hard work to make ends meet. The Guardians, however, considered that on his Own admission he was able to pay the amount asked for.—An order for the amount asked for was granted. A COSTLY THROW.—Richard Hughes, a youth, described as a clerk, reQiding at 46, Bewsey-stre t, was summoned for as- saulting a little boy named Elijah Radburn.—lt appeared that the defendant was passing a point where a little boy and a number of children and ycuths were playing, and a stone was thrown at him. In a moment of passion he picked up a stone, which be threw in the direction of the youths, and it hit the complainant, causing a contusd wound on the side of his head. The child had to be attended to by Dr. Cannell.—The Berch dismissed the case on payment of 259 6d costs. NEGLECr OF Wohir.—Sarah Bibby, Rose-yard, Dial-street, was summoned by Wm. Gallop, fustian cutter, Buttermarket- street, who claimed 12s 6d from defendant for neglect of work. —Complainant said that defendant left his employ on the sth June without finishing a piece for which he had paid her 78 6d She had now come back to her work, and he believed she would finish the piece, but he claimed 5s for the frame standing while she was away.—An order was made for the defendant to pay the amount claimed at Is per week.
