HUTTON. On F. riday, at the Liverpool County Sessions, John WQann (19), Thomas Robinson (22), and William Fleet (20), laboumrt, were acquitted of a charge of indeomtly anaulting 'Margaret Lester, at Huyton, on the 26th ult. AL&RMING CARRIAGE ACCIDENT AT HUTTON.— 0 0 Wednesday afternoon, an accident of an alarming character happened to Dr. Packer and a lady named Lacomber. The doctor had been paying a visit at the mansion of Mr. Thos. Cope, JP. Returning down the drive, one of the front wheels of the carriage came off, overturning the vehicle, and throwing the lady and gentleman on to the bank. The horse toot fright, and dashed on to the entrance gate. The vehicle, coming in collision with the gateway, was smashed to atoms. The horse, which received a severe cut on its hind leg, was then stopped. The docter and Miss Lacomber (who was driving at the time) escaped with only a few. , scratches and a shaking. HUYTON QUARRY. , At the Liverpool County Sessions, on Friday, William Knox (54), gardener, charged with wounding his son, ; Samuel Knox, at Huyton Quarry, on the 19th May, was acquitted.
FRODSHAM.

RUNAWAY HORSE AT FRODSHAIC—COBSideTabIe excite-I m,mlt. was caused on Wednesday afternoon by a horse bolt- ing with a trap from opposite the TrinPy Chapel, and proceeding at a furious rate down the main street to a little past the Town Hall, when its mad flight was fortunately stopped through it falling down. The roan in charge, it appears, had takes the bridle off tu give the horse a drink of water, when it su,ldeoly started as above stated. DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES AT ASTON SCROOL.—With the view to encourage regular attendance of children at school the Aston School Board decided to present a prize for at- tendince to all children who had attended 90 per cent and upwards out of the number of possible attendances during the school year, and Friday last was fixcl for the presentation of the prizes, when a good tea was given by Mrs. Coke, of Aston Lodge, to all the children attending the school numbering about 100. After tea had been done full justice to, the Rev. E. Marsden, vice-chairman of the Board, made an appropriate speech, and H. Coke, Esq , afterwards dis- tributed a book to each of the 16 successful scholars for their regular attendance and efficiency at examination and class work. When the prises had been distributed the children amused themselves in the schoolroom until half- past seven, when each child received a bun and bag of sweets, and the proceedings closed with three hearty cheers to Mrs. Coke for her excellent treat. • GOLBO RNE.
NANFWIOH.

At the Chester Assizes, on Monday, John Mottram pleaded guilty to the charge of having, at Nantwich, on the 26A1 ultimo, stolen ten skins, the property of Simnel Bind, and received a sentence of six mouths' imprisonment with hard labour. Thomas Carroll, who was charged with being a partner in the offence, was acquitted. Elizabeth Salmon, aged 21, a servant, pleaded guilty to the charge of having, at Nantwich, on th ) 3rd instant, obtained three mantles, value £5 183. from Arthur Windsor, by false pretences. A sentence of six months' imprisonment with hard labour was imposed. The first meeting of the creditors of William Manning (trading as Manning Bros.), of Nantwich, grocer and urovi- sion merchant, was held at the Royal Hotel, Crewe, on Tuesday. The statement of affairs as submitted by the receiver, Mr. James Eckersley, chartered accountant, Cross- street, Manchester, showed total unm.cured debts £2,548, and assets, less preferential claims £1,778. No offer being made, liquidation was resolved upon, and Mr. Eckersley was ap- pointed trustee, with a committee of inspection. Mr. Marten was entrusted with the registration of the resolutions, and appointed solicitor to the trustee. NORTH WICH.

CONSERVATIVE _TEA PARTY AND BALL AT GOLBORNE.— A tea party and ball in connection with the Ciolborne Con- servative Club were held in Mr. Brewis's school-room, on Saturday evening last. About 100 members and friends sat down to an excellent tea; among the ladies presiding at the tables being Miss Atkinson, Mrs. Bearden, Miss Mary Ann Dearden, Mrs. Foster, Miss Taylor, and Miss Ashcroft. After tea Mr. H. Arnott briefly addressed the company, re- marking that the club was in a prosperous condition at the present time, as they were better off now than they were at the same time last year. A selection of dance music was excellently played on a violin by Mr. Scholes, and the party thoroughly enjoyed themselves in dancing to its strains. At intervals songs were capitally given by Mr. Vim. Jen- kinson and Mr. T. Mort, Miss Taylor very efficiently pre- siding at the pianoforte. After a pleasant evening had been spent, Mr. Woolacott moved a vote of thanks to the ladies who presiled at the tables, and the motion was seconded by Mr. Kay. It was heartily accorded, and the proceedings were brought to a close. HALE WOOD.

MPOWELL V. VERDIN AND OTHERS.—This case was beard at the Chester Assizes this week. Messrs. Swetenham Q.C., and Clement Higgins, were for plaintiff, and Mr. M'lntyre, Q C., M.P., was for defendants. The plaintiff who is a salt manufacturer and merchant at Northwich, sought to recover compensltion for damages sustained by a flat belonging to Messrs. Verdin and Sons, salt manufac- turers, Northwich, sinking a flit belonging to the plaintiff, in which was a cargo of salt. The jury found for plaintiff, damages £lB9 19s. 21

FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—About half-past One on Saturday morning, John Kendrick, 40 years of age, who resided in Halebank-road, Halewood, died from injuries he had received on Tuesday, the 17th instant, whilst uncoup- ling some wagons on the railway extension which is being made between Dittou and Halebank by the London and North-Western Railway Company. HAYDOCK.

VIOLENT ASSAULT ON A POLICE-CONSTABLE AT BIL- LINGE.—On Monday, at the Wigan County Police Court. two colliers, of St. Helens, named James Swift and James Moran, were charged with wounding P.C. Hodgson, at Bil- linge, while in the execution of his duty.—lnspecter Kier, who prosecuted said about half-past ten on Sunday night Police-constable Hodgson was passing Mr. Heald's farm- yard, in Billinge, when he heard voices as if some people were talking together. He went in to see who they were, and found the two prisoners and another man not in custody. There was a man who had charge of the farm ordering them away. The constable asked what business they had there, and they told him it was no part of his duty to inquire. Seeing one of the prisoners had something in his pccket, Hodgson asked him what he had got, and without any more ado Swift struck him in the mouth. He closed with the man, and was knocked down, and while down Swift kicked him in a vital part, and Moran kicked him all over his body, which was very much discoloured. The man not in custody seized hold of a bottle and struck Hodgson on the head with it, in fact, so violent was the blow, that it broke the bottle. Hodgson, with the assistance of the farmer, de- tained the two prisoners, but the other man got away. Afterwards, Hod4sorr went to Dr. Anderson, of Billinge, who dressed his wounds.—Tbe prisoners were remanded until Wednesday, when they were again brought up, and ulti- mately committed for trial at the Liverpool assizes.

ASSAULT BY A WOMAN AT RAINHILL.-At Prescet Pett• -f I Sessions, on Tuesday, a woman named Ellen Crawley was charged with assaulting William Johnson. Mr: M..actsenzie appeared for the complainant, who is a bro0 maker ato r., Rainhill. Defendant was a servant or I) u3elteoper for Mr. 'c Wright, of Rainliill. On the 2nd ast, deferraant went to 'ff.: for some atticles which she complainant's Ileum to innu alleged were in the possslon of complainant's son's wife, and on being told 'that the things were not in their posses- sion, and nevr had been, she persisted in saying that they were, and refused to go away without them. She used most filthy and 4basive language to defendant's wife in the pre- sence of his family. Johnson, who was in his workshop upstairs, hearing the disturbance, came down to ascertain the cause, and asked defendant to go away, but she refused, and called him foul names. He thereupon took her by the arm to lead her out, when she struck him just over the eye with a house-door key, inflicting an unpleasant cut, and while he was wiping the blood from his face she struck him three or four times with her clenched fist. Complainant's son then took her away.—A witness stated that defendant "fought like a man."—Defendant was tined 10s, and Ps Oct costs.

For tof the Newton Improvement Commissioners, a meeting of the ratepayers of Newton was held in the District Infants' School, Market-street, E erlestown' on Wednesday afternoon. Tae chair was occupied by Mr. Thomas Stone (returning officer at the election of Commissioners), and there were also present: Messrs. W. F. Gooch, B. B. Glover, J. Fair- dough, J. E. Worsley elaw clerk), R. Brierley "(clerk and surveyor). H. Houghton. G. Appleton, Burchall, &c. The CHAIRMAN observed that they had first to announce the election of four Commissioners. In accordance with the proper course, notices were issued to the ratepayers calling their attention to the fact that four Commissioners were retiring, and giving notice that nominations of candidates were to be delivered to him as returning officer on a certain date. He only received four nominations—and the four retiring Commissioners were again proposed. He attended at that school at nine o'clock that morning to open the poll, and he received a vote for each person. He therefore thought it was his duty to announce that Messrs, Gooch, Emmett, Glover, and Forster were duly elected for the ensuing term of three years. Mr. WORSLEY observed that the next business was the passing of the accounts of the Board for the year ending 25th March last. Printel copies of the accounts were dis- tributed to tbose present. The Highway Fund Account showed receipts amounting to £2,557 9s 4d, including a balance of £476 12s 84 in hand at the commencement of the year. The expenditure amounted to £2,080 123 44, leaving a balance of £476 17s. in hand, while the amount of uncollected rate was £399 183 id. The General Improvement Fund showed a balance of £947 2e 6/1 in hand at the commencement of the year, and this, added to the receipts, brought up a total of £2,878 103 5/ I. At the Manchester Assizes, on Thursday, a waiter in the Queen's Hotel sued Mr. Farrar, a gentleman of large pro- perty at Market Drayton, for damages for an assault. The defendant was taking breakfast one morning at the hotel, and noticing that there was no sugar on the table told the waiter that if he had to ask for anything else he would "kick him out of the window" The waiter said he had better not do this, whereupon the defendant knocked him down with a blow in the face and blackened his eyes. The jury awarded the plaintiff £lOO.

div.head: HE ATLEY.
div.p: HE ATLEY.

SAD DROWNING CASE AT HEATLEY.—Mr. T. J. Ridgwav, coroner,held an inquest at the Green Dragon Inn,Heatley,on Monday, touching the death of Francis Patrick .Feets, springmaker, of Maiach9ster, who was found drowned in the river Bollin, at Heatley, on Sunday evening.—John Peets identified the body as that of his brother. He last saw him alive on Saturday night, when he told him that be and a man named Shelmerdine intended to come to Heatley on the follow;ng day to fish. Deceased was subject to fits, but he (witness) did not think that Shelmerdine was aware of it.— Alfred Shelmerdine, Cricket-street, Moss-lane, Hulme, said that deceased and himself came to Heatley on Sunday morning, arriving at Heatley station about half-past eight. Deceased seemed in good health. They went to the Green Dragon Inn, and afterwards went in company with a man named Smith to fish in the Boffin. Smith and he were with deceased about half an hour, when they passed him and went further down the river. He did not see him alive again. Deceased was quite sober.—Edward Holt, Sandy. hue, Lynam, said he was fishing in the Bollin on Sunday afternoon. About four o'cl,,ck he found a rod on the bank and a line in the water. He then saw a hat in the water, and subs fluently found the body in water about 2ft. Gin. derp. 'I he body was against the side, and the grass near that point was flattened as though deceased had rolled down into the water. One band was clenched with a piece Of

div.head: OVER
div.p: OVER

At the Chester Summer Assizes, on Monday, Edwin Littlemore. alias Hulse (33), pleaded guilty to the charge of having, at Over, on the 23rd ult., stolen £2 18s. 11d., the money of Mark Peters, and was sentenced to three months' imprisonment with hard labou,. PORTICO.

ACCIDENT NEAR PORTICO.—On Tuesday afternoon, Mr. Barras, foreman at Mr. William Longten's stone quarry, Portico-lane, met with a serious accident. While attending to some machinery one of his hands waq caught by a cog wheel and very b idly crushed and lacerated. He received attention from Dr. O'Hara at the Workhouse hospital.

div.head: PRESTON BROOK.
div.p: PRESTON BROOK.

PRESTON BROOK PRIMITIVE METHODIST CIRCUIT.—OR Sunday sermons were preached at the Greenvray-road Chapel, by the Rev. L. 'Miles, who has been appointed col- league to the Rev. J. Pickwell, in succession to the Rev. D. Schofield. His labours in the circuit he has just quitted have been very successful, and his acquisition to local Methodism is hopefully spoken of. On Monday evening a tea party and meeting was held to mark the commencement of Mr. Miles ministry. The Rev. J. Pickwell presided, and delivered an appropriate address of welcome. Addresses were also given by several members of the congregation, and the Rev. L. Miles made a speech in reply. Like his predecessor, Mr. Miles will reside at Frodsham.

div.head: R A.INFORD.
div.p: R A.INFORD.

AWAY FROM HOME.—James Stewart, an ohl and descrepit man, was fined 5s and costs at the St. Helens Police Court, en Saturday, for having been drunk and incapable in Crab- street on the previous day.—Superintendent Johnston said the prisoner was a farm 1 ibourer, and lived at Red Cat, Rainford, and seemed to have a habit of coming into St. Helens to get drunk. RAINFULL.

RAINHILL WxsLEYA.ii—S-c-no-o—ts—.---The annual excursion in connection with these schools took place on Wednesday. The scholars with their parents and friends, to the number of about 200, journeyed in conveyances to the Child o of Hale, where ample provision was made for their entertain- ment, and a happy day was spent in a variety of amuse- ments. .

BLUE RIBBON TEA PARTY AT RAINHILL.—Upwards cf 150 of the scholars attending the different schools at Rain- hill who have donned the blue ribbon, were liberally en- tertained on Tuesday afternoon by Mrs. Owen, Rainhill. An excellen tea was set out in the field on the Top-o'-the- Hill, where the annual flower show is usually held, and the weather being fine the children and nurnerons friends heartily enjoyed themselves. COWARDLY ASSAULT AT RAINHILL. Michael Hora, a collier working at Carr's colliery, Whiston, was charged at Present, on Tuesday, with assaulting Ann Bell, a single woman. Complainant stated that she worked on the pit brow at Present colliery, Whiston. She was an orphan and lodged with Mrs. Mary Moore, next door but one to prisoner, in Present. About half-past five o'clock on Tuesday morning, she had just left the door of her lodgings to go to work when defendant stole noiselessly behind her in his bare feet, seized her by the hair of the head, and thumped her unmercifully on the head and ribs. She screamed for help and defendant ran up an entry. She returned to her lodgings, and after- wards, when on the way to her work, defendant met her and threw half a brick at her. Previously defendant and his sister had broken the windows of the house in which she lodged.—Defendant was fined 5s and costs.

div.head: URDISTON.
div.p: URDISTON.

URMSTON AND FLIXTON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.— The anniversary sermons were preached on Sunday morn- ing and evening by the Rev. Stephen Hartley, pastor of the Congregational Church at Besses-o'-th'-Barn. The church was tastefully decorated with flowers and plants. The children's annual flower service was held in the church in the afternoon, when a musical service was given by the Sunday scholars and the church choir, strengthened for the occasion by the presence of members of the Sale Congrega- tional Church choir and of the choir of Eccles Presbyterian Church. The children each brought a bunch of flowers, and the flowers contributed will be distributed by the Man- chester Ladies' Flower Mission amongst the Manchester hospitals. Mr. Tarbeck, of Manchester, acted as reader. The appearance of the flowers, which were staged near the pulpit, was very effective. There were large congregations at the services, and collections were made in aid of the church funds. "

It seems that the ueLootleo-'4le to Earlestown last week end and stopped at thmile he 0L her nephew, Thomas Large, Tamworth-street, tee Viadoalld his wife proceeded to London for three days on oh. Iteentie' Works trip. About half-past nine o'clock on .01,dret ~aY night she was getting the supper ready for two nierl of i .7itid.a brothel. of Large's, when she began to corn- 'Bt, ki_u.Pain about her stomach. She was assisted to the '4548,1' rbyt shortly afterwards to be assisted into the "Ighbour named Mrs. Newman. As Mrs.

Cornea rapidly grew worse, Dr. Handyside was sent for, but before his arrival the poor woman had expired. ' —An inquest on the body of the deceased was held at the Oddiellowe Arms, Legh-street, on Thursday afternoon, be- fore Mr. T. W. Barker, coroner. The following evidence was given :—Henry Littler, a collier residing at Stubshaw Cross, said the deceased was his mother. She was the wido' of John Comes, late of Lyme-street, Haydock, and was 55 yors of age. She resided with him (witness), but for about a fo:tnight she had been staying at 21, Tamworth- street, Earlestowti. She had lived with witness for about eight months past. j was eight or nine years since her husband died. She had c+: joyed pretty good health, and he had never heard her complain of anything. He last saw her alive on Sunday afternoon at his hon;:.• .She then appeared all right. She had never been attended aT any doctor.— William Aiton Large said he resided with his brher at 21,;J Tamworth-street. Mrs. Cornea had stopped there for a fortnight attending to his brother's children. She had had very good health during that time to all appearance. She was taken unwell about half-past nine on MondaV night, and complained of a pain in her stomach. He assisted bet Put - side in the yard, and left her in the closet. He called two neighbours named Mrs. Newman and Mrs. Woodyer, the former of whom brought Mrs. Cornea out of the closet into the kitchen. The deceased was then moaning, and he (wit- ness) went for Dr. Handyside. When the latter arrived the woman was dead. He (witness) did not know what the cause of death was. In reply to a juror, witness said Dr. Handyside came in about a quarter of an hour after he went for him.—Mrs. E. Newman, 23, Farnworth-street, deposed that about 10 o'clock on Monday night she was called in Large's house by the last witness. She found Mrs. Comes in the closet complaining of a pain across her stomach. She (witness) called for her husband, and together they carried her into the kitchen, an 4 laid her on the floor. She could not then speak, as she was unconscious. She died in about quarter of an hour. She appeared to be convulsed, and " twitched " her arms when she was in the closet.—Mrs. Mary Woodyer, 30, Tamworth- street; stated that she was called into Large's house shortly after ten o'clock on Monday night. She was on the floor, and Mrs. Newman was supporting her. She was present when she died about half-past ten.—The Coroner briefly summed up, remarking that it was highly probable from the symptoms that the woman's heart was affected, and the only conclusion they could arrive at was that she died from natural causes.—The jury then returned a verdict of "Death from natural causes."

THE JUNIOR CLUBS, RUNCORN —On Saturday a match was played between the Trinity and the Parish Church Juniors at Runcorn. Score: Trinity 57, Parish 43. ST. BARNIBAS (2ND TEAM) V. TRINITY (2ND TEAM).—A match was played between the above clubs on Saturday, and resulted in an easy victory for Bt. Barnabas. The scores were ;—St. Barnabas (second team), 54; Trinity (second team); 30. WINWICE V. LGWTON.—This match was commenced at Win- wick on Saturday, but was abandoned as a drawn gams owing to rain after about an hour's pay. The home team commenced batting, and lost three wickets for 53 runs, of which Mr H Longton claimed 32 (not out). RUNCORN PERSEVERANCE V. RUNCORN EXCELSIOR. This match was played on the ground of the latter, and resulted in a victory for the Perseverance by 11 runs. Littlem ore and Leathwood scored well for the Perseverance, and Harrison for the Excelsior. Score : Perseveranze 29 and 46, Excelsior 24 and 27. ST. ELPHIN'S V. WARRINGTON CLARENCE.—A match between the above clubs was played on Saturday on the ground of the former, and resulted in a victory for the ht. Elphin's by 38 runs. Hardman and Barnes batted well for the home team, scoring 20 and 15 respectively. t cores : Bt. Elphin's, 55; War- rington Clarence, 17. The bowling of Knowles and Worthington was very good ; the former in 14 overs had 7 maidens and took 7 wickets for 12 runs, the latter 1 In 10 overs had 6 maidens and took 3 wick As for 4 runs, A substitute lent by Latchford made 15 runs out of the 43. Albinson senior and junior bowled well, and Green and Smith did execution in the fielding for the win- ners. Few and Clegg did well for the losers Score :—Tub Thumpers, Ist innings 40, 2nd innnings 55; Co-operative, Ist Innings 43, 2nd innings 44. MR. D. Q. STEEL'S ELEVEN V. ST. HELENS. This match was, on Saturday, played in the Recreation Cricket Ground, B yundary-road, St. Helens, between Mr. D. Q. Steel's eleven and eleven of St. Helens and district, under cireumstances of the most unfavourable kind as far as weather was concerned. With a few slight intermissions rain fell during the whole afternoon, and this, it is hardly necessary to say, both , lessened the number of spectators and damped the enjoyment of those who were present. There was, however, under the circumstances a very fair attendance. With regard to the play, the appended scores wilt show that the visitors carried away the palm as far as scoring went. It wit , however, be also I noticed that this is not so much due to their general superiority over the home team as to the very fine play of Mr. I D. Q. Steel himself. The Bt. Helens players were the first to take the wickets, and were ultimately disposed of for the score I of sixty-five. The best scores we, e made by W. Gerrard and F. ryo, but, the bowling of the visitors, and particularly that I of Mr. Steel, was too deadly to permit of any isrge scores being made, especially when the fielding was so carefully attended " to. In the naxt innings, as we have said. Mr. Steel's batting I was the most notable feature. After having seen almost the I whole of his c lleagues come and go. he was himself caught out by Parr, having made the magnificent score of 108. The bowling of the St. Helens team, notwithstanding numerous changes. was ineffective, only one of their opponents being lo,,wled out. This, however, was to some extent compensated for by very smart fielding, there being several excellent catches. In a second innings, which, however, was cut short by the rain and the lateness of the evening, the St. Helens players made a better stand, and had it teen possible to con- tinue would probably have recoverski some of their lost ground. FLOWER SHOW AT WHISTON. The annual exhibition of flowers, fruits, and vegetables in connection with the fluyton and Whiston Cottagers' Horti- cultural Society, was held on Saturday afternoon, in a field adjoining the Lathams, Whiston, the residence of Mr. Mc- Clure, treasurer of the society. The society is under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, and is supported by many of the gentlemen of the neighbourhood, the show being confined exclusively to cottagers in Whiston and Huyton. Has hag so small an area from which to draw the produce of the flower and kitchen gardens it is necessarily not on a very large scale. Nevertheless, the show on Satur- day, like the inaugural one last year, bore most gratifying testimony to the care, taste, and industry with which the cottagers cultivate their little plots of land and use their windows for the rearing of flowering plants. Over a hun- dred prizes were offered for competition, and for each prize there was a keen competition and an abundant supply of exhibits. Perhaps the most interesting part of the show was that of vegetables, in which department the cottagers showed to great advantage, collecting together a profusion of really two and well-grown products. The show of flowers was also extremely good, and there was a fair collection of fruits. In the vegetable department the variety and excellent quality of the potatoes shown was especially remarkable. The exhibition was held in a com- modious marquee, and the exhibits were staged by the committee with much taste. The arrangements generally being in every respect of a most satisfactory character. Mr. McClure, the treasurer, and Mr. Err Lee, the hon. secretary, aided by a numerous committee, omitting no detail which could contribute to the comfort of visitors, the convenience of competitors and the success of the show generally. The only unfortunate thing about the whole affair was the weather, which could scarcely have been worse for such an occasion, but notwithstanding the storm of wind and rain which prevailed during tbe whole of the afternoon and even- ing there was a large attendance,amon. others present being Mr. and Mrs. Willis and family, Mrs. 'Duncan and family, Mr. and Mrs. Whittle, Mr. and Mrs. McClure. The band of the Prescot Rifle Volunteers was present, and played during the afternoon. The possibility of a dance on the green sward was destroyed by the weather, but in the evening, when most of the elder visitors had gone home, this was compensated for by a dance by the younger visitors, in the marquee the exhibitors clearing out their exhibits for the purpose, the conservatories of Mr. McClure affording tem- porary accommodation for many of the plants. The judges were Mr. Durant, of Prescot, and Mr. Watkin, of Huyton, both of whom were emphatic in their praise of the show, and whose decision gave every satisfaction. The following prizes were awarded : Collection of Vegetables : 1 Joseph Rainford, 2 James Perrin. Collection of potatoes : 1 Joseph Rainford, 2 William Rainford. Six kidney potatoes: 1 George Lester, 2 James Sharpies. Six round potatoes; 1 William Rainford, 2 Joseph Rainford. Twelve spring sown onions: 1 Joseph Lyon, 2 Jos. Rainford. Twelve eutunin sown Onions: 1 John Lyon, 2 Wm. Mason. Six carrots or turnips : 1 Wm. Rainford, 2 Joseph Rainford. Six turnips: 1 Richard Mason, 2 Wm. Rainford. Three cabbages : 1 Thomas Lawrenson, 2 Joseph Rainford. Two red cabbages: 1 Thomas Smith. Cauliflowers: Richard Mason. Three lettucps : 1 John Mason, 2 Wm. Mason Twelve pods of broad beans: 1 John Lyon, 2 Thomas Rimmer. Cucum- bers: 1 and 2 Wm. Yates. Turnips: 1 Miles Smith, 2 Wm. Painford. In one of the despatches the British directors report to Earl Granville the terms M. de Lesseps was willing to concede as to a reduction of the rate of tonnage dues in consideration of receiving as- sistance, financial and otherwise, from her Majesty's Government, towards the construction of the second canal. RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

- - On Thursday, this society completed the 21st year of its existence, and the important and interesting event was declared to the outside public by the display of flags and bunting at the Central Stores in Church-street, Runcorn. Since its establishment on July 26th, 1862, the society has despite several serious obstacles, gone on from success to success, and its business is now one of the most extensive and remunerative in the locality. Its shops in Runcorn are the great goods depots for. the working classes, and the branches in Widnes are scarcely less successful. To show how rapidlyc the society has.advanced, we have only to state that the operations of the society for the first half year produced a profit of only £75 Oa 3d, whilst the last half yearly balance sheet showed that the dividends paid on purchase for that period amounted to no less a sum than £4,606 lOs 6d. It may be of interest to sketch briefly the origin and progress of the undertaking. The establishment of the society dates from a lecture delivered to a meeting in Runcorn by Mr. Richard- son, of Worsley, who inspired his hearers with some of the spirit which animated the Rochdale pioneers. A fund with which to start operations was subscribed, and a com- mittee consisting of the following was formed :—Messrs. William Rhodes, William Rushton, John Bailey, Thomas Riley, John Clucas, Robert Royle, Joseph Hughes, Jonah Evans, John Howard (treasurer), and James B. Arthur (secretary.) A shop in Devonshire-square was rented, and, with mingled feelings of hope and fear, was opened on July 26. 1862. " Walk before you run" was a proverb which the promoters evidently well understood, for the value of the stock was only £BO. For a considerable time the members of the committee performed much of the manual labour connected with the business, following out the example set them by the originators of the co-operative movement. Success attended their efforts. A larger shop had to be rented, and the society was enrolled under the Industrial and Provident Societies' Act. For the half-year ending December, 1864, a dividend of 3s. in the £ was de- clared, and it is doubtful if the profits of this period have ever been exceeded. As time went on the premises in Church-street were built, but an incident occurred before their completion which showed the earnestness and determi- nation of the members of the society. The contractor for the building, after erecting the outer walls, becamebank- rupt, but the committee, undeterred by so untoward an event, set themselves the task of completing the structure, and by meeting nightly and working zealously they accom- plished the work. The building cost upwards of £1,600, but it has since been considerably enlarged; the society gradually extending their operations,and dealing in boots and shoes, and coal, and establishing a drapery club and a bakery. Then then opened a store in Hutchinson-street, Widnes, and in 1873 opened a penny savings bank, which is now one of the most successful branches of the society's , orulertakinu. In April 18!T4, the society built a new store in Ditton-road, winnes, at a cost or £1,200, and two branches are now carried on in the same town. In 1877, a second store was built in Runcorn, near the railway station at a cost of £BOO. so that, including the mein store in Church-st, the society carries on six establishments with great success, a fact which will not be dispated when it is stated that the total sales for the half-year ending December last amounted to £33,509 8s 101, being an increase of £5,094 14s 4.1 over the corresponding period in 1881. The attainment of the society's m ijority affords a favourable opportunity for offering a suggestion, which we will take advantage of. The co-operative societies in Lancashire, with very few ex- ceptions, appropriate a certain proportion of the profits, say 14- per cent, towards educational purposes, and establish excellent newsrooms, valuable libraries, and success- ful science and art classes. We will not advise the Runcorn Co-operative Society to follow this example entirely; but in Runcorn we have a free public library, which, although it has passed its first year in a most admir- able fashion, is nevertheless much in want of funds Could not the society, out of the large profits it makes, contribute a handsome annual subscription to the Free Library, where it is sure to get well spent, and where the members of the society will participate in the benefits as well as the general public-? Thus, without undertaking educational matters themselves, the society would worthily aid one of the most important educational institutions in the town; and we feel confident the members would not object to the slight reduc- tion in their dividends which such a donation would cause. We trust the committee will favourably consider the sug- gestion.

AULTERATED SPIRITS AND MILK AT WIDNES. \At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Andre, Car- ragher, of the Arch Hotel, was summoned' for s'Siling rum which was not of the substance and quality aemanded.— Inspector Barnett stated he purchased th.ree half-pints of rum from the defendant, and proved tint the usual tech- nicalities had been observed.—Superintendent • Barker for- warded a sample of the spirits to Dr. Campbell Brown, who tertified that it was a mixture of rum, burnt sugar, and water, 29 per cent under proof, and four per cent. weaker than the utmost limit allowed by the Amendment Act. The proportion of sugar was excessive.—Mr. Barker ob- served that the practice of adding water to increase the bulk of the spirits meant considerable profit to the vendor. , —The Bench fined the defendant 403, and costs 193.--- Owen Tansey appeared in answer to a summons charging him with selling, on the 3rd July, a pint of Irish whiskey whicb was not of the substance and quality demanded, to Inspector Barnett.—Dr. Campbell Brown certified that he had analysed the spirit, and was of opinion that it was a mixture of whiskey and water, 34 per cent. under proof. It was nine per cent. weaker than the utmost limit allowed by the Amendment Act.—The clefendant was fined £3, and costs 193.—John Clare, of the Rine' o' Bells, Earn- worth, was charged with selling, on the 3rd July', three half-pints of rum, not of . quality demanded, to Inspector Barnett. —A sample had been forwarded to the public analyst, who certified that it was a mixture of spirits, burnt sugar, and water, of strength 301 under proof, and 51 per cent. weaker than the utmost limit allowed by the Amendment Act.—A fine of 403 and costs 193 was imposed.—Patrick Osborne, keeper of a milk house in Eleanor-street, was summoned on a charge of selling to Inspector Barnett one pint of new milk which was not of the nature and substance demanded.—lnspector Barnett on the 3rd inst. purchased the milk from the defendant's wife, in whose presence it was sealed up. It was then forwarded to the public analyst, who certified that the milk contained 15 per cent. of water.—Defendant stated that he sold the milk in the same condition in which he purchased it from the farmer.—Mr. Willis, the chairman, said the Bench con- sidered the case proved, and they must see that the defen- dant was more careful in selling his milk. The responsi- bility lay, with him, as he could make considerable profit by selling his milk watered to the extent of 15 per cent.— Defendant: But I did not do it, sir.—Mr. Willis: You are responsible. Your remedy lies with the party you buy your milk from, and you must proceed against him for selling milk that is adulterated. We might fine you £2O, but we shall only fine you 40a and costs 193.

CHILD EMIGRATION TO CANADA. The committee appointed to deal with the proposed emigration of 50 children to Canada reported that the Local Government Board had intimated they wculd rot be pre- pared to allow the guardians to send out so many as 50 in the present year, and requested to be furnished with details of the proposed expenditure of LW upon each child. The committee also reported that Mr. Newsome bad had an interview with the Local Government Board, who would be willing to allow 25 to be sent out, and they recommended that 25 children be selected.—Mr. NEWSOME said he waited upon the Local Government Board when he was in London, after receiving information from Mr. HARTLEY that they would not consent to 50 children being sent out. They said that only 300 children wild be sent out in one year, and the year was still young, and it would be unfair to send so many from Prescot Union as there were many other unions to be considered. They gave him to understand that they would favourably consider 25 being sent out, and as far as he could gather they held out strong hopes that the effective steps the Dominion were taking would °pea a 'large field for pauper children.—Mr. LEATHERBARROW Said he should offer his strongest opposition to any attempt to sever a brother and sister. If one was sent to Canada and the other was left at Kirkdale they might never meet again. —Mr. NEwsomz handed to the Chairman a list of 32 children selected by the committee out of which to choose 25.—Mr. HALL moved that Mr. Bicknell be requested to go to Pantasaph and bring the children included in the list to Kirkdale for final selection by the committee.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS seconded the motion.—Mr. MEADOWS was at a loss to know why children should be removed from Pantasaph. It was a good institution, an the children were kept there for less money than they could , keep them at the workhouse.—Mr. NEWSOME said with re- ference to Mr. Leatherbarrow's remarks that the object of 'the committee was to select children between ten and twelve years of age with their own consent. They could not sand a sister of rive with a brother of twelve.—Mr. MEADOWS: Then you would not send either of them in that case ?—Mr. NEWSOME: No.—The Rev. T. FINEGAN said the consent of the children was necessary before they could send them to Canada, but the proposition before the Board was that they should remove a certain number from one institution to another before they knew whether they were willing to go to Canada or not. If they got the children from Pantasaph to Liverpool and they did not wish to go, what was their position then? They should first ascertain from Pantasaph whether the children were willing to go, and then remove them. It struck him that point had been overlooked, and they were going into the thing pre- cipitately.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS: It appears this is another case of distrust of a committee. I will be glad if the Chairman will put the resalution as it was passed by the committee.—The CHAIRMAN pointed out that the resolution of the committee was incomplete, as it did not specify the children who were to be sent out. He then put the motion moved by Mr. Hall, and seconded by Mr. Chambers, and it was lost.—Mr. NEWSOME: In what position are we now P—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS: I should think the posi- tion of the committee is that they will retire and leave it to others. I for one do.—The CHAIRMAN: I think it would have been better if the committee had brought in a definite resolution giving a list of the resolution. Is there any other business? The better plan will b 3 for the committee to meet and select 25 children.—Mr. HALL: Leave it in their hands to select.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS : What! after the treatment we hive received from the Board! Have we no respect for ourselves P--The CHAIRMAN: Then I will go on to the next business. Oh, that is the last business gentlemen.—The board then rose without passing any resolution on the subject which accordingly drops for the present —Before separating, it was resolved on the motion of Mr. NEWSOME seconded by Mr. HALL to hold the annual revision of the outdoor relief lists. . 1 ia I illii
PARR'S BANKING COMPANY.

Yesterday, an extraordinary general meeting of this com- pany was held at the Bank, Winwick-street, Warrington, fur the purpose of sanctioning the declaration of an interim dividend, electing a director, and concluding the ordinary business of the company. Mr. J. C. Parr (chairman) pre- sided, and there were also present the following :—Direc- tors: Lord Delarnere, Sir G. Greenall, Col. J. F. Greenall, Col. McComuodale, Messrs. P. Stubs, E. Greenall. H. Wood- cock, N. Eckerslev, J. Pearson, A. Hewlett, John Thompson, U. W. Meade-King, and 0 tkt Rharenntaora__. __ Messrs. H. W. Kelly (Dublin), A. Mackie, Jno4Thomson, W. Sharp, John Lythgoe, H. Milling, John White, John E. Davies, Dr. Beaman, Robert Davies, W. Silcock, jun.,T. Fairhurst, John Dun (general manager), and J. Murray (secretary). The directors report was read by Mr. Dun, as follows: " Thedirecwrs have had before them the audited balance sheet of the bank at 30th June, 1883, and they beg to report that the profits of. the half year, after providing amply for all bad and doubtful debts, have been satifactory. The directors recommend that there be now declared, for the half year ending 30th June, an interim dividend at the rate of £l5 per cent, per annum, free of income tax, and payable on and after 3rd August. After providing for this dividend there remains a considerable balance, which is car- ried forward to the next account. The position and prospects of the business continue to be in every way satis- factory. The business acquired from the National Bank of Liverpool has so far fully answered the expectations formed of it. Mr. T. P. Parr -having resigned his seat at the Board, the directors recommend that Mr. Cecil F. Parr be now elected a director in his place." The CHAIUMAN then said the business that day was, as they all knew, almost purely formal. It was not their custom to publish a balance sheet more than once a year, and therefore he did not think it necessary to go into figures. and would content himself with stating generally that the position and prospects of the businesseontinued to be in every way satisfactory. The money lodged had increased, and the number of accounts had also in- creased, and this was, he might say, well distributed over the whole area of the bank. Of course he said this irre- spective of their addition of the Liverpool business. The bad debts, he was glad to say, continued to be small in number and unimportant in amount. As regarded their Liverpool businesa, the six months which had elapsed had given them very satisfactory experience of its working, but they would quite understand that half a year was too short a period to enable the directors to say much as to the course and progress of the business or its ultimate result. They

I would be much better able to judge in December next when the balance sheet and abstract of accounts were before them, and, therefore, beyond saying this, he should leave the subject until that time came. He should content himself with asking those present to confirm the recommendation of an interim dividend, which he need hardly say had been amply earned. The next notice on the paper was the elec- tion of a director to fill the vacancy which had been caused by the resignation of Mr. T. P. Parr. He might say a few years ago Mr. Cecil Parr, who was a member of the board, resigned his position in order to fulfil an avocation elsewhere. His resignation was accepted with very great regret, for he proved himself a valuable member of the board and had done good service, especially on the select committee. He was now about to return to settle in this neighbourhood. and had expressed a wish to be rein- stated upon the board of the bank, and for that reason his eldest brother was prepared to .create a vacancy which the shareholders would be asked to fill up. Mr. Thomas Parr. in sending in his resignation had written a letter which he was desirous of having read to the meeting, and with their permission he would ask Mr. Dun to read it. Mr. Dux then read the following :—" I have already in- timated my intention of resigning my seat on the board of Parr's Banking Company, and now write to gild' formal I notice of same. My sole reason for this step is to create a vacancy on the board and on the Select Committee for my brother, Mr. C. F. Parr, and I take it with great regret, and solety because I think it to the interest of the bank, as he will .live nearer and give more time to the business than I should do. But if a vacancy occurs on the board, I should be most anxious to join it again should the directors see fit to recommend me to the shareholders for re-election." The Cmarnatax movi,d the adoption of the report, which was seconded by Colonel GREENALL (the deputy chair- man), and carried. The CHAIRMAN proposed, Lord DELAMERE seconded, and it was carried, that as recommended by the directors, an interim dividend at the rate of 15 per cent. per annum free of income tax be now declared, payable on and after the 3rd August, at the bank or any of its branches, or by Messrs. Glyn, Mills, Currie, and Company, London. Mr. JOHN WHITE proposed that Mr. Cecil Francis Parr be re-elected a director.
Mr. W. SmARP seconded the proposition, which was agreed to. On the motion of Councillor MAcKIE, seconded by Mr. R. DAVIES, a vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman, and the meeting terminated.

DESPOILING THE FARMERS,—A lad named John Woods, aged 12 years, was on Tuesday fined 7s. 7d. in all at the St. Helens Police Court for having stolen turnips from the fie2d of William Sumner, farmer, Moss Bank. Mr. Sumner said a great deal of thieving was done in his turnip fields oy boys, and he brought the prisoner there an a warning to <others.

T. CHAMBERS :My pro- TM ihaila of Mr. Dennis O'Connor will give the Parnel- position includes that.—Mr. LEATltEnnalutOW : I sisould lite party another seat. At the last election only one mum- like to know who registered the boy, and by what means ber of the party, Mr. Sexton, was nominated ; but, as he they found out the entry was incorrect. We have no infor- stood at the top of the poll, there is little doubctliat, if both mation yet why the boy should be turned over to Roman seats had been contested in the Nationalist interest, betls Catholicism.—The CHAIRMAN: It must be by his own desire. would have been carried. I understand that Mr. Parnell has He is now a free agent, and if he desires to be educated as a a candidate ready for the vacancy, and that his name will Roman Catholic the master must see that he is educated as be announced ia the course of a day or so. a Roman Catholic.—The motion was agreed to. With regard to the sale of the Duchess of Teck's furni- ture and china, I am told that a few years ago the greater part of the Duchess of Edinburgh's trousseaus was sold by auction in London as "the property of a lady of rank." The Duchess's wedding outfit was on a scale of truly Eastern magnificence, and as it would not have been pos- sible to wear out one-half the articles in ten years, her frugal husband thought it would be as well to convert the bulk of the collection into money, and many of the gar- ments were exposed and sold while still marked with her monoeram and coronet. I have reason to believe that the Treasury, with the con- currence of the Postmaster-General, has agreed to recom- mend to the House of Commons that the tender of the London and North-Western Railway Company, for the con- veyaece of the Irish mails from Holyhead to Dublin, be accepted. The amount of the company's tender is £76,000, and they have proposed to accelerate the arrival and des- patch of the mail boats. Communications on the subject will be made to Parliament some day next week, when a good deal of protestation may be expected from Irish mem- bers of every diverse political view. What liquidation means, a recent announcement makes clear. Overend and Gurneys failed on May 11, 1866—that is, more than 17 years ago. On Wednesday next the share- holders will have returned to them ss. per share. At the end of 17 years, after so many persons have lost fortunes, after so many have lost their lives, the settling is still going on; and even now the business is not wound up. It will not be wound up for some time to come. So big an affair must of course take a long while. But one cannot help doubting whether greater expedition would not have been possible under a better system. Scotland may perhaps learn to remember that when the Scotch Tenant Right Bill was discussed in committee on Thursday not a single Conservative leader put in an appear- ance from noon until six o'clock. By thus punishing Scot- land for being so Liberal at the late election, the Conserva- tive chiefs show their hopelessness of making Scotland Con- servative at the next election. They surrendered their position of leaders to Mr. Balfour and Mr. Chaplin, who seemed to enjoy by anticipation the honour of sitting on the front bench, and really looked as well there as Sir Richard Cross and Mr. James Lowther. A great scandal is shaking the shipping world just now. A member of one of the mutual underwriting clubs has been discovered in league with a shipbuilder to charge the insuraace clubs 33 per cent. more than the actual cost for repairs, and to have put the difference into his own pocket. A man of high position, a county magistrate, and a wealthy man into the bargain, is the offender. All the clubs in the country we represented at a meeting held to discuss the situation. It was proposed to prosecute the man for the re- turn of the money, but a better plan was discovered. "Boy- cott him," was the cry, and now no ship on which his name appears can be insured for any premium he may like to offer, however large. The statement that a vessel recently left Alexandria bound for I iverpool laden with 56 bales of rags, chiefly col- lected in Cairo and the villages adjacent, has called forth very strong comments from the medical papers. The Lancet, in particular, urges that the duty of the Govern- ment is to send out a steam tug to meet the vessel, with instructions that her cargo shall be thrown overboard and the ship disinfected. There seems to be a good deal of doubt as to the authenticity of the statement that any such consignment was despatched, but if so, there is no doubt the Government will be on the alert to prevent its being landed at any English port. In getting Mr. Norwood to move the amendment to the Tory resolution, the Government has acted with great dis- cretion. Mr. Norwood is a "Jingo," a shipowner, and a very independent supporter of Mr. Gladstone. Throughout the debates on the Eastern question be was the friend of Lord Beaconsfield. He was one of the leaders who got the Suez Canal agreement withdrawn. The Tories quoted him as the very man who would go into the lobby with them. 'rheir chagrin may be imagined when they find him des- cribing their motion at the present moment as highly inex- pedient. His great freedom of opinion in the past gives Mr. Norwood great power over Liberal opinion, and he will be followed by nearly every one of the malcentents who secured the failure of the agreement. Matthew Webb is only the latest of the victims of fool- hardy experiments, from Daedalus downwards. The man who leapt from a pyramid on London Bridge into the Thames was killed. De Groof, who nine years ago tried to fly at Chelsea, fell before the church in Roberts-street, I and was killed. The inventor of the famous parachute tried it in Paris; the parachute doubled up like an umbrella, and he was killed. Of deaths from ballooning there are innumerable examples, from those of F, zier and Romain in 1785 to that of Lieutenant Harris in 1824, and that of Sadler in 1825; and the death of Mr. Powell last year. Then there was the death of Coching, who descended from a balloon in a parachute at Vauxhall, just after the Queen's accession in 1837. But such mad tricks seem hardly to be preventable. When the balloonists took animals with them, they were made amenable. But their own lives the law does not regard as within its scope. A singular and interesting relic or archaic philology has Sc.. brought unaer the notice of the Palestine Exploration Fund. The relic consists of pieces of skin containing por- tions of the book of Deuteronomy and the Commandments, in Phenician characters, which have been recovered from a Bedouin tribe located on the eastern side of the Jordan. The period to which the writing is to be referred is presum- ably identical with that of the Moabite Stone—that is, about 800 BC. he documents are in elips, the skin being dark and discelouted, and the writing requiring to he brought out with spirits of wine. They have been examined by Mr. Bond, the principal librarian of the British Museum; Dr. Ginsberg, Mr. Aldis Wright, of Cambridge; Dr. Horning, of the Manuscript Department of the British Museum; Dr. Van Starland and Mr. Ernest Bridge, severally of the Hebrew and Assyrian Departments of the same institution, and-other gentlemen. If their genuineness can be established, they will tend considerably to modify several passages of Deu- teronomy as at present received in the Old Testament. It is evident that the Government is of opinion that there can be no movement by the Suez Canal Company towards the construction of a second canal without fresh authority, and that if the Egyptian Government did not claim such reference the Porte would do so. The Sultan's Government appears quite convinced of its own rights in the matter, and though not very powerful in itself, yet the Porte can and will arouse all the alarms of diplomacy before any definite action is taken. There is good reason to believe that the German Government has given an expression of opinion, and that while it is not unfavourable to English influence in Egypt, it is strong in the view that in any increase of the means of communication between the two seas, regard should be had not only to vested pecuniary interests, but also and especially to international concerns. All this is thought to show that there can only be a momentary repose in the con- nection of the British Government with the subject. If the Suez Canal Company propose operations it is likely they will be at once checked by diplomatic action, in which the authority of this country must be paramount.
THE VIADUCT4WORKS TRIP TO LON- DON AND BLACKPOOL.

The annual trips in connection with the Viaduct Wagon Works, Earlestown, belonging to the London and North- Western Railway Company, took place last week, the places visited being London and Blackpool. The question" Where shall we go? " is left for the men themselves to decide, and a few weeks ago the two places mentioned were again selected by overwhelming majorities. As on the last occasion, the Metropolis was the centre of attraction, and tickets thereto were very early asked for. This cm scarcely be wondered at when it is stated that return tickets for three days were offered at so low a figure as 45., while the tickets for one day were only 3s. During the past week an extraordinary demand far the tickets was made, and the supply fell far short. Notwithstanding an extra number which were issued, scores of persons were dis- appointed in their efforts to secure tickets for the three days. while others offered sums considerably above that mentioned in order to get them. As it was, about 2,500 persons were conveyed to London in four well-filled trains. The first train left Earlestown shortly before 12 o'clock on Friday midnight, the rain, which had been falling during the afternoon and evening, at that time coming down very heavily. Nest came two trains from Edge Hill and St. Helens Junction, which took a considerable number of the trippers from Earlestown; while the last train left Farles- town shortly before half-past one. The crush and throng at Earlestown station was something extraordinary. The trains were announced to start from the Goods Station siding, and an hour and a half before the departure of the first train people commenced to gather round the gate. As the minutes passed by the " waiters " swelled into a crowd, and when the gate was opened about eleven o'clock there was a rush for seats in two empty trains in the siding. The car- riages were soon filled, but the excursionists in one of the trains were considerably disappointed in having to wait over two hours before a start was made. All the trains proceeded on their journey without mishap or accident, and everyone arrived safely at their destination. The weather cleared up about six o'clock in the morning, and with the exception of one or two showers of short duration, remained favourable for the trippers on each of the three days. In every respect the trip was a most suc- cessful one, and the majority of those who pro- ceeded by it, went in for seeing as many of the sights of London as was possible, the chief places of attraction being the Houses of Parliament, Westminster Abbey, St. Paul's Cathedral, Crystal Palace, the Tower of London, and the Fisheries Exhibition at south Kensington. The day trip arrived back at Earlestown shortly before four o'clock on the Sunday morning, the trips leaving London on the Monday night arriving at Earlestown in quick succession after half-past three o'clock on the Tuesday morning. The trip to Blackpool was comparatively well patronised, about 700 persons paying a visit to the popular sea-side re- sort. They were conveyed in a train leaving Earlestown at six o'clock on the Saturday morning, and, notwithstanding the showery weather, the majority of the trippers thoroughly enjoyed their outing. The excursionists to Blackpool had the opportunity and privilege of returning on one of several trains which ran there on the Monday, and a few availed themselves of it: but nearly all returned by the I"special," which left Blackpool about seven O'clock on Saturday night.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. In the House of Lord; on Tuesday evening, Lord Win- marleigh moved that the Standing Order of the House made on the 2nd March be dispensed with and the Manchester Ship Canal Bill be road a second time. The Earl of Redes- dale, in opposing. said the ieason for the order was that private bills might COine on at a time when it was possible to appoint good committees to consider them. He believed it _ .

l would be impossible to appoint a committee to whom it , would be proper to refer this bill. Their lordships were, he t added, asked to pass a bill which was avowedly imperfect, , as the ship canal could not be constructed until another Act was passed next session. If they allowed legislation to be conducted in this manner abuses of a serr,ous character would arise. Lord Winm trleigh made f i forcible appeal in support of the bill; and the Earl of Derby, as a member of the House and not on behalf of the Government, spoke in favour of the motion. The motion was carried by 87 votes to 24, and the bill was read a second time.

In the House of Lords, on Thursday, the Earl of Cork I gave notice that he would move that the following noble 1 lords be appcinted a Select Committee on the Manchester j Ship Canal Bill :—The Duke of Bedford, the Earl of Devon, ! the Earl of Aberdeen, the Earl of Camperdown, and Lord 1 Carrington.—The Earl of Redesdale said he could not agree to the appointment of that committee. He did not consider it a proper committee, for he knew how it would decide the question. They ought to be able to appoint a committee J from a full attendance of the House, and at this period of I the session, as was well known, the attendance always fell j off He had stated the other day that he did not think j it was possible at this period to appoint a proper corn.- l , mittee to consider such an important bill as this, and he : adhered to that opinion. He should feel it is duty to oppose the appointment of the committee—Earl Granville said he could not understand the ground of the noble Earl's opposition, and certainly the noble Earl's observations were not in accordance with that regularity and order which he felt it his duty to promote. As the Lord Chancellor pointed out the other day, those who had voted in favour of the ap- pointment of a committee this session were not in the slightest degree committed to the merits of the bill. The merits of the bill were not gone into by any member of the House, except the chairman of committee (Lord Redesdale). For himself, he (Lord Granville) had really not made up his mind in the slightest degree whether it was desirable to have a ship canal to Manchester or not. —The Earl of Redesdale said if he had taken an unusual course in giving notice of his intention to oppose the appointment of the committee, the noble earl had also been irregular in giving notice of his motion.—The Earl of Cork said that after the vote taken the other day, he had felt it his duty to endeavour to obtain a committee to inquire into this very important question. He bad con- ferred with the Earl of Redesdale and the Earl of Lathotn, but had been unable, with one exception, to obtain assistance from the other side of the House. He had thought it only courteous to inform their lordships of the names of the committee. The time for depositing petitions against the bill has now expired, and it appears that twelve petitioners will oppose by counsel the preamble when it comes before a select com- mittee of the House of Lords. Th, principal petitioners are the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, the Corporations of Liverpool and Birkenhead, the London and North-Western Railway, the Midland Railway, the Great Western Railway, the Cheshire Lines C immittee, the Shropshire Union Rail- way and Canal Company, and the Upper Mersey Navigation Commissioners.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Thurs- day, Mr. W. Tyrer presiding. There were also present the Revs. T. Chambers, J. Barnacle, and T. Finegan, Messrs. Meadows, Hall, Leatherbarrow, Newsome, Fisher, A shton, Matthews, Lowe, Jackson, Buckley, Dobai!, Syder, Marsh, Swift, Kenwright, and P. Longton.

AN I:NV:JONI PI3RONASIC. It was reported that the new conveyance purchased for the use of the Board bad been sent to Kirkda.le with nine children. After the children had been landed the horse started off down the school yard, overturned and smashed the conveyance and then ran away into the street. Mr. conveyance, thought the matter should be inquired into, the horse and cmveyance having cost M.—Mr. MEADOWS explained that Mr. Leatherbarrow, Mr. Birchall, and himself were deputed to buy a conveyance and horse, and Mr. Birchall and he (Mr. Meadows) went to Liverpool one day and bought a conveyance, Mr. Leather- barrow not being able to meet them. He thought the con- veyance was a very suitable one, and cheap at the price they paid for it. That day month Mr. Birchall Saw him at the meeting of the Board and said he had heard of a horse in St. Helens, that he thought would suit,that he had known it for some time and they ought to buy it. Be (Mr. Meadows) reminded Mr. Birchall that Mr. Leatherbarrow was one of the three deputed to make the purchase, and sug- gested that Mr. Birchall should bring the horse to the work- house on the following Tuesday morning, when the House Committee met, and no doubt Mr. Leatherbarrow would make it convenient to attend. However, the next day there was a meeting of the Assessment Committee, and Mr. Birchall came to that meeting and told him he had bought the mare. He (Mr. Meadows) replied that neither Mr. Leatherbarrow nor himself had been asked anything about it, and they would have liked to have seen it before it was bought. " Oh, yes," Mr. Birchall replied, " I have bJught it, and it is all right." He (Mr. Meadows) said that seeing they had only an old man to look after it a mare was not suitable, and he would not have bought it on any account. He went to look at it, and said he considered it dear at .E4O. Mr. Birchall said" Well, I have a verterinary surgeon's cer- tificate, and it is passed as sound." He (Mr. Meadows) said he did not believe it was sounO. ard he considered the money far too much, and he did not agree to the mare being purchased. Last Board-day he understood a cheque would be drawn, and be then told the chairman and members of the Board that he objected to the mare being purchased.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS: Is it advisable to go further without Mr. Bir- chall being present ?—Mr. HALL: Perhaps Mr. Leather- barrow will give some explanation.—Mr. LEITHERBARROW said he would much rather not make any remarks as Mr. Birchall was not here. He could not get to St. Helens. but he said ne had such reliance upon Mr. Bircball's practical experience ann 3unginetit Ltia hc .ouia ocr.o. to Intm chasing the horse provided he got a veterinary's certificate. —The CHAIRMAN: You see there was the consent of the majority of the committee.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said he quite agreed to the matter being left over till Mr. Birchall was present, otherwise be should be inclined to move that the horse be sold. If any Guardian had not seen the debris of the carriage they should see it. If they kept that horse they would have nothing to do but to buy carriages. It was stated that the driver of the horse was an old man, and Mr. DOBELL remarked that he was not competent to look after it.—Mr. MATTHEWS said that if the same precautions had been taken to get a good driver as well as a good horse, the accident might not have happened.—lt was resolved to let the matter stand over until Mr. Birchall was present.

div.head: 311STER'S REPORT.
div.p: 311STER'S REPORT.

The MAgren reported that there were 438 inmates of the workhouse as against 441 in the corresponding week of last year. There were six innntes suffm.- ing from smallpox, and four from typhus fever. The Master's report book also contained a memorandum by Mr. Henry Stevens, Local Government Board inspector, that he had inspected the workhouse except the infectious hos- pital, and found it clean and orderly. Its fittings and contents generally were in good repair, and some valuable improvements had been carried out both inside and outside the buildings.

div.head: RELIGIOUS DIFFICULTY.
div.p: A RELIGIOUS DIFFICULTY.

The Local Government Board transmitted for considera- tion a letter from Father Henry respecting the entry on the creed register of the workhouse of a boy named Henry But- ler. The lettex stated that the boy was entered as belonging to the Church of England, while it appeared that he was a Roman Catholic, and he naturally desired the entry to be amended. The boy's baptismal certificate and a letter from his mother to the priest at St. Mary's, Widnes, showed that op to his seventh year he was educated as a Roman Catholic, and from enquiries made of the said priest, the Rev. Jas. Clarke, it appeared both the father and mother of the boy were Roman Catholics. Moreover, for two years after his admis- sion to the Workhouse the boy was under his (Father Henry's) own care and instruction, and attended the Catho- lic services at Portico, and was looked upon by the whole house as a Catholic. It was only two years ago, when all the school children were removed to Kirkdale, that in con- sequence of the wrong entry he was put among the Protes- tant children. Father Henry requested the Board to comply with the boy's request to have the entry amended.—The CHAIRMAN said it appeared from en- quiries wnich had been made that the boy was over twelve years of age, and bad left the school and gone into the service of a firm of tradesmen, so tbat neither the Local Government Board nor the Guardians had any control over him. If he desired to be regarded as a Roman Catholic he could attend the Roman Catholic services, and it would be for Father Henry to communicate with his employers or get the priest in the neighbourhood where he was to look after him.—The Rev. T. FINEGAN: Is he free to select his own religion ?—The CHAIRMAN: Yes.—The Rev. T. FINEGAN -said the boy's master was under an obligation to see that he attended the services of the religion he belonged to, and if the boy was erroneously admitted into his service as belonging to the Church of England, his employer would feel himself bound to see that he attended the Church of England services. If, therefore, the Guardians found there was a mistake they should cor- rect it as far as they could. They should show the em- ployer that a mistake had been made.—The CHAIRMAN said they could not amend the entey .in the creed register, but they could write to the master informing him that there had been a mistake, and that the boy was a free agent.— Mr. LEATHEREARROW : Would it not have been more courteous if Father Henry had written to this Board before writing to the Local Government Board ?-The CHAIRMAN : I think so.—Mr. VEWSOME : Should you not first inform yourselves that you have all the facts of the case ?—The CHAIRMAN : If the boy wishes to attend the Roman Catho- lic worship be is a free agent.—The Rev. T. CH&MBERS The afair may .be settled at once if wc com- municate with the man with whom the .boy is Placed and say there has been a mistake. I

move that • the Master be written to, and the circumstances placed before him, and that the boy be told that as he was brought tup a Roman Catholic it is his duty now to attend the Roman Catholic worship—ln answer to Mr. Hall, the CLIAIRmAN said the boy was entered in the creed register in April, 1877, as belonging to the Church et England.—Mr. HALL: Then how .c an we say be is a Roman Catholic? Has he been a Protestant ever' since ?—The Rev. T. CHAMBELIS: By accident.—Mr. HALL: It would have prevented all these communications if Father Henry had written to the Guardians first.—The Rev. T. CILAWBERS: I think 80.—The Rev. T.
